# The Quasiparticle Ansatz for Relativistic Continuous Matrix Product States

## Abstract

The Relativistic Continuous Matrix Product State (RCMPS) ansatz introduced in [1] is a translation-invariant variational ansatz intended to approximate the ground states of gapped one-dimensional relativistic Quantum Field Theories directly in the continuum limit and in infinite volume. In this work, we develop an ansatz, referred to as the Relativistic Quasiparticle (RQP) ansatz, for the low-lying one-particle excitations of the RCMPS vacuum, as well as for solitons interpolating between two distinct degenerate vacua. The corresponding energies of these states can be obtained as the eigenvalues of an effective Hamiltonian. The RQP ansatz generalizes constructions used in the Matrix Product State and Continuous Matrix Product State literature. We apply the RQP ansatz to the sine-Gordon model and find good agreement with results from integrability for both the soliton and breather masses. We also apply the RQP ansatz to the $\phi^{4}$ theory, in both its $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ -preserving and $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ -broken phases, and determine the spectrum of particles and solitons. This enables us to determine the parameter regime for which multiple stable particles exist.

## 1 Introduction

Matrix Product States (MPSs) [2] and Hamiltonian lattice methods have become increasingly important tools in understanding strongly coupled dynamics in $(1+1)$ d quantum field theories (QFTs) (see [3, 4, 5] for reviews). MPSs are ansätze for many-body wave functions of lattice systems that exhibit area law entanglement entropy, which make them efficient approximations of gapped ground states. MPS methods have been used to study gauge theories with fermionic matter [6, 7, 8], scalar field theories [9], conformal field theories [10, 11], and, importantly, an array of real-time observables [12, 13]. Furthermore, the MPS ansatz can be extended to model excitations using the quasiparticle ansatz [14] and estimate bound state masses in the aforementioned models [8, 15]. Since MPSs are formulated on a spatial lattice, the quantum dynamics is governed by a lattice Hamiltonian that approximates the continuum one as the lattice spacing is taken to zero. Fermionic theories are especially well-suited for such numerical lattice studies because the fermion statistics naturally yields a finite local Hilbert space at each lattice site. Moreover, in $(1+1)$ d, one can avoid some of the fermion doubling that plagues higher dimensional lattice theories. On the other hand, lattice realizations of bosonic theories exhibit infinite-dimensional local Hilbert spaces that must be truncated in numerical implementations. This truncation introduces an additional cutoff, and one needs to make sure that the low-energy observables of interest converge as one increases the truncation parameter [9].

An elegant way of dispensing with the lattice is the Continuous Matrix Product State (CMPS) introduced in [16], which formulates an ansatz analogous to the discrete MPS for a non-relativistic QFT directly in the continuum limit. Using the CMPS ansatz, the issue of finiteness of local Hilbert spaces in bosonic theories does not arise since, in continuous space, multiple occupancy is equivalent to single occupancy of infinitesimally neighboring points [16]. CMPSs have been applied to both fermionic and bosonic relativistic QFTs, but they require the introduction of explicit counterterms for the ground state search to converge [17, 10]. For the case of scalar field theories with non-derivative interactions, this situation is somewhat unsatisfying, as it is well known that such theories can be rendered finite by normal-ordering [18]. This issue was addressed more recently in [1] with the introduction of Relativistic Continuous Matrix Product States (RCMPSs), which adapt CMPSs to relativistic scalar field theories making the ultraviolet (UV) finiteness manifest. The key insight of RCMPSs is to employ a basis of states derived from the energy eigenstates of the free massive scalar field theory. RCMPSs automatically encode properties of relativistic QFT such as the short-distance behavior of two-point functions, making them better starting points for approximating interacting vacua. The RCMPS framework allows for efficient simulation of ground state properties directly in the continuum limit and at infinite volume. The method was initially used to study $\phi^{4}$ theory [1] and later the sine-Gordon and sinh-Gordon models [19], defect QFTs [20], the $O(2)$ model [21]. This framework was also used to constrain the spectral density through vacuum correlators [22].

The RCMPS ansatz has the same structure as the CMPS ansatz, so it is natural to attempt to adapt CMPS constructions to the language of RCMPS. One such construction is the quasiparticle ansatz [23], which models a single particle- or soliton-like excitation as a local perturbation of a vacuum state as encoded by a CMPS. The quasiparticle ansatz was used to determine the dispersion of particles in non-relativistic QFTs but has, to the best of our knowledge, not been applied to relativistic systems. On the other hand, the quasiparticle ansatz for MPSs has proved to be a powerful tool in determining excitation spectra in relativistic gauge theories [8, 24, 15].

In this work, we adapt the quasiparticle ansatz to RCMPSs, which we will refer to as Relativistic Quasiparticle (RQP) ansatz. The RQP ansatz allows us to study both the spectrum of particle-like excitations as well as solitons of $(1+1)$ d scalar QFTs. We first apply the RQP ansatz to the sine-Gordon model, which is integrable [25] and exhibits a rich spectrum of particles and solitons whose masses are known exactly. The numerical results from the RQP ansatz are in good agreement with integrability results. Furthermore, we find that the RQP ansatz accurately reproduces the relativistic dispersion relation required by the Lorentz invariance of the QFT. This agreement demonstrates that RCMPSs and the RQP ansatz are good approximations of relativistic states despite neither of them being manifestly relativistic.

We also apply the RQP ansatz to the $\phi^{4}$ theory. As the coupling is taken from weak to strong, this theory undergoes a phase transition that belongs to the Ising universality class [26]. We observe that the mass gap closes at a value of the coupling that is in agreement with other estimates in the literature [27]. The RQP ansatz gives full access to the spectrum of particles and solitons, and it can be used to determine for which parameters stable excitations can exist. In particular, we find that deep in the strong coupling/ $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ -broken phase, the spectrum contains two stable particles and a soliton (and associated anti-soliton), in agreement with semi-classical predictions and earlier numerical evidence [28, 29, 30].

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the RCMPS ansatz and how to use it to compute expectation values in scalar field theories. In Section 3, we define the RQP ansatz and derive the necessary formulas to determine the spectrum of particles and solitons. The formalism is applied in Section 4 to the sine-Gordon and $\phi^{4}$ theories. Technical details are contained in the Appendices.

## 2 Relativistic Continuous Matrix Product States

We begin by reviewing the RCMPS ansatz and establishing notation and formalism that will serve as the basis for the derivation of the RQP ansatz.

### 2.1 The RCMPS ansatz

RCMPSs were first introduced in [1] for studying relativistic $(1+1)$ -dimensional field theories with a single scalar field $\phi$ and non-derivative interactions. Such theories have Lagrangian and Hamiltonian densities of the form11 1 We denote the coordinates by $x^{\mu}=(t,x)$ , and we use the Minkowski metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}=\text{diag}\,\{1,-1\}$ to raise and lower space-time indices.

$$ {\cal L}=\frac{1}{2}\dot{\phi}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}-V(\phi)\,,\qquad{\cal H}=\frac{1}{2}\pi^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}+V(\phi)\,, $$

where $V(\phi)$ is the scalar potential and $\pi=\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial\dot{\phi}}$ is the canonical momentum conjugate to $\phi$ . We may assume that $V(\phi)$ has a global minimum at $\phi=0$ where $V(0)=0$ , so that

$$ V(\phi)=\frac{1}{2}m^{2}\phi^{2}+V_{\text{int}}(\phi)\,, $$

where $m$ is the mass of the field $\phi$ around the $\phi=0$ vacuum and $V_{\text{int}}(\phi)$ is the interaction potential, whose Taylor series expansion around $\phi=0$ is assumed to start at cubic order. The methods we will develop have general applicability to potentials that can be expressed as sums of polynomials and exponentials in $\phi$ , with the concrete applications presented in Section 4 being restricted to the $\phi^{4}$ and sine-Gordon theories, for which

$$ \begin{split}\text{$\phi^{4}$ theory:}&\qquad V_{\phi^{4}}(\phi)=\frac{1}{2}m^{2}\phi^{2}+g\phi^{4}\,,\\
\text{sine-Gordon theory:}&\qquad V_{\text{sG}}(\phi)=\frac{m^{2}}{\beta^{2}}\left[1-\cos(\beta\phi)\right]\,.\end{split} $$

The two examples (2.3) consist of families of theories parameterized by the dimensionless parameters $g/m^{2}$ in the $\phi^{4}$ case and $\beta$ in the sine-Gordon case22 2 The mass parameter $m$ serves only as a renormalization scale as will be explained in Section 4.1.

At the quantum level, the precise definition of the field theory (2.1) requires more care. To be specific, we will work in the Schrödinger picture, where both $\phi$ and $\pi$ are time-independent quantum operators obeying

$$ [\phi(x),\pi(y)]=i\delta(x-y)\,. $$

Since $V(\phi)$ is a composite operator, it requires regularization. A standard procedure in $(1+1)$ -dimensional QFTs without irrelevant interactions is to use a normal ordering prescription with respect to a free scalar field of some mass $\mu$ .33 3 The parameter $\mu$ used for normal ordering is not necessarily equal to the mass $m$ mentioned above. (Different choices of $\mu$ correspond to different regularization prescriptions.) As usual, the normal order product $N_{\mu}[\cdots]$ of any number of $\phi$ and $\pi$ operators is defined by expanding these operators in Fourier modes of a free scalar field of mass $\mu$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\phi(x) \displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk}{2\pi}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\omega_{k}}}(e^{ikx}a_{k}+e^{-ikx}a_{k}^{\dagger})\,, \displaystyle\pi(x) \displaystyle=-i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{\omega_{k}}{2}}(e^{ikx}a_{k}-e^{-ikx}a_{k}^{\dagger})\,, $$

with $\omega_{k}\equiv\sqrt{\mu^{2}+k^{2}}$ , and then ordering the $a_{k}$ and $a_{k}^{\dagger}$ operators under the $N_{\mu}$ sign such that all $a_{k}$ appear to the right of all $a_{k}^{\dagger}$ . Normal ordering then provides a precise definition of our theory whereby the dynamics is given by the Hamiltonian

$$ H=\int dx\,\mathcal{H}\,,\qquad{\cal H}\equiv N_{\mu}\left[\frac{1}{2}\pi^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}+V(\phi)\right]\,. $$

Note the normal ordering $N_{\mu}[\cdots]$ distinguishes the Fock vacuum $|0\rangle$ as the state annihilated by all of the annihilation operators, $a_{k}|0\rangle=0$ . This state is the ground state for the specific case $V(\phi)=\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}\phi^{2}$ .

Regardless of the value of $\mu$ , the commutation relations (2.4) imply $[a_{k},a_{k^{\prime}}]=[a_{k}^{\dagger},a_{k^{\prime}}^{\dagger}]=0$ and $[a_{k},a_{k^{\prime}}^{\dagger}]=2\pi\delta(k-k^{\prime})$ , which, in turn, imply that the Fourier transforms of $a_{k}$ and $a_{k}^{\dagger}$ ,

$$ a(x)\equiv\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk}{2\pi}\,e^{ikx}a_{k}\,,\qquad a^{\dagger}(x)\equiv\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk}{2\pi}\,e^{-ikx}a_{k}^{\dagger}\,, $$

obey the commutation relations

$$ [a(x),a(y)]=[a^{\dagger}(x),a^{\dagger}(y)]=0\,,\qquad[a(x),a^{\dagger}(y)]=\delta(x-y)\,. $$

The commutation relations (2.8) are identical to those of a non-relativistic (complex) scalar field $\psi(x)$ :

$$ [\psi(x),\psi(y)]=[\psi^{\dagger}(x),\psi^{\dagger}(y)]=0\,,\qquad[\psi(x),\psi^{\dagger}(y)]=\delta(x-y)\,. $$

Of course, $a(x)$ defined in (2.7) should not be interpreted as a non-relativistic scalar field.44 4 The interpretation of $a(x)$ and $a^{\dagger}(x)$ is that, in the free theory $V(\phi)=\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}\phi^{2}$ , the operator $a^{\dagger}(x)$ creates a single quantum of the field $\phi$ localized within a region centered at $x$ whose size is comparable to the Compton wavelength $\sim\mu^{-1}$ , and the operator $a(x)$ annihilates such a quantum. Nevertheless, the fact that the equations (2.8) and (2.9) are identical allows one to consider an analog of the CMPS ansatz introduced in [16] for non-relativistic field theories by simply replacing $\psi\to a$ in many of the equations in [16]. The result is the RCMPS ansatz introduced in [1], which we now review.

For QFTs defined on the entire real line, the RCMPS is a translation-invariant ansatz that can be used to approximate the ground state. It is parameterized by two complex $\chi\times\chi$ constant matrices $Q,R$ , and two complex $\chi$ -dimensional vectors $V_{+\infty},V_{-\infty}$ :

$$ |Q,R\rangle=V_{+\infty}^{\dagger}\mathcal{P}\exp\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\Bigl(Q\otimes\mathds{1}+R\otimes a^{\dagger}(x)\Bigr)\right]V_{-\infty}|0\rangle\,. $$

Here, the tensor product is between the $\chi$ -dimensional virtual space on which $Q,R$ act and the physical Hilbert space of the QFT, the path ordered exponential $\mathcal{P}e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,(\cdots)}$ is defined such that the operators with larger $x$ labels appear to the left of those with smaller $x$ labels, and the vectors $V_{+\infty},V_{-\infty}$ serve as boundary conditions for the virtual space of the path-ordered exponential. The parameter $\chi$ is known as the bond dimension, and it serves as the truncation parameter of the ansatz. As we will explain shortly, the matrices $Q$ , $R$ and the boundary vectors $V_{+\infty},V_{-\infty}$ must obey certain conditions in order for the state (2.10) to be normalized. Furthermore, as we will explain, the precise choices of $V_{+\infty},V_{-\infty}$ do not affect any physical quantities computed in infinite volume.

Note that one can also construct other variants of RCMPSs. One such variant that will be very useful in the following discussion consists of the more general family of states

$$ |{\bf Q},{\bf R}\rangle=V_{+\infty}^{\dagger}\mathcal{P}\exp\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\Bigl({\bf Q}(x)\otimes\mathds{1}+{\bf R}(x)\otimes a^{\dagger}(x)\Bigr)\right]V_{-\infty}|0\rangle\,, $$

where ${\bf Q}(x)$ and ${\bf R}(x)$ are non-trivial functions of $x$ . Other generalizations of RCMPSs can be obtained by considering compact spaces and boundaries [31, 20].

### 2.2 Normalization conditions

To determine the conditions obeyed by $Q$ , $R$ , $V_{+\infty}$ , $V_{-\infty}$ for the RCMPS (2.10) to be normalized, we use the fact that the more general states (2.11) have the overlap (see Appendix A.1 for a proof)

$$ \begin{split}\langle\mathbf{Q}^{\prime},\mathbf{R}^{\prime}|\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{R}\rangle&=(V_{+\infty}^{\dagger}\otimes V_{+\infty}^{\prime T})\mathcal{P}\exp\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\Bigl(\mathbf{Q}(x)\otimes\mathds{1}+\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{\mathbf{Q}}^{\prime}(x)+\mathbf{R}(x)\otimes\overline{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}(x)\Bigr)\right]\\
&{}\times(V_{-\infty}\otimes\overline{V}^{\prime}_{-\infty})\,,\end{split} $$

where the tensor product is between $\mathbb{C}^{\chi}$ and $\overline{\mathbb{C}}^{\chi}$ . Taking $\mathbf{Q}(x)=\mathbf{Q}^{\prime}(x)=Q$ , $\mathbf{R}(x)=\mathbf{R}^{\prime}(x)=R$ , and $V^{\prime}_{\pm\infty}=V_{\pm\infty}$ gives

$$ \langle Q,R|Q,R\rangle=\left(v_{+\infty}\middle|\exp\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\mathbb{T}\right)\middle|v_{-\infty}\right)\,, $$

where we defined the transfer matrix $\mathbb{T}$ and the boundary vectors $|v_{-\infty})$ , $(v_{+\infty}|$ :

$$ \mathbb{T}\equiv Q\otimes\mathds{1}+\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{Q}+R\otimes\overline{R}\,,\qquad(v_{+\infty}|\equiv V_{+\infty}^{\dagger}\otimes V_{+\infty}^{T}\qquad|v_{-\infty})\equiv V_{-\infty}\otimes\overline{V}_{-\infty}\,, $$

and we removed the path ordering symbol since the matrix appearing in the integrand of the exponent is $x$ -independent.

The factor $e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\mathbb{T}}$ can be interpreted as the limit

$$ \exp\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\mathbb{T}\right)=\lim_{L\to\infty}e^{L\mathbb{T}}\,, $$

and it can be evaluated using the spectral decomposition of the $\chi^{2}\times\chi^{2}$ matrix $\mathbb{T}$ . Let $\lambda_{k}$ , $k=1,\ldots,\chi^{2}$ be the eigenvalues, and $|r_{k})$ and $(l_{k}|$ the right- and left-eigenvectors, obeying the eigenvalue equations

$$ \mathbb{T}|r_{k})=\lambda_{k}|r_{k})\,,\qquad(l_{k}|\mathbb{T}=(l_{k}|\lambda_{k}\,. $$

The eigenvectors of $\mathbb{T}$ can be chosen to be orthonormal, i.e. $(l_{k}|r_{k^{\prime}})=\delta_{kk^{\prime}}$ , but the left- and right-eigenvectors are in general not related to each other by Hermitian conjugation. As shown in [31] in the case of CMPSs55 5 Technically, the (R)CMPS has to be “injective” for this result to hold (see [31]). However, a generic (R)CMPS is injective, so it will have this property., for matrices $\mathbb{T}$ of the form (2.14), the eigenvalue with the largest real part (also referred to as the dominant eigenvalue) is unique and purely real. Let us take this eigenvalue to correspond to $k=1$ , and simply denote it by $\lambda$ and its corresponding eigenvectors by $|r)$ and $(l|$ . Using the spectral decomposition $\mathbb{T}=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}|r_{k})(l_{k}|$ , it then follows that $e^{L\mathbb{T}}=\sum_{k}e^{L\lambda_{k}}|r_{k})(l_{k}|\approx e^{L\lambda}|r)(l|$ for $L\to\infty$ . As we can see, the factor $e^{L\mathbb{T}}$ that we need to evaluate does not have a finite limit as $L\to\infty$ unless $\lambda=0$ . We therefore choose the $Q,R$ matrices such that $\lambda=0$ ,66 6 Such a choice can be easily made: from any given pair of matrices $(Q,R)$ for which the dominant eigenvalue $\lambda$ does not necessarily vanish, one can construct the new pair $(Q^{\prime},R^{\prime})=(Q-\frac{\lambda}{2}\mathds{1},R)$ for which the dominant eigenvalue vanishes. in which case $e^{L\mathbb{T}}$ approaches the projector $|r)(l|$ as $L\to\infty$ ,

$$ e^{L\mathbb{T}}\approx|r)(l|\qquad\text{for $L\to\infty$.} $$

Thus, from (2.13), we infer that the RCMPS is normalized provided that

$$ \langle Q,R|Q,R\rangle=({v}_{+\infty}|r)\times(l|v_{-\infty})=1\,. $$

This is a condition that must be obeyed by the boundary vectors $V_{\pm\infty}$ . For future convenience, we will further restrict these boundary vectors such that each factor in (2.18) equals one separately:

$$ \displaystyle\left(v_{+\infty}\middle|r\right)=1\,,\qquad\left(l\middle|v_{-\infty}\right)=1. $$

To summarize, we restrict the parameters $Q$ , $R$ such that the largest eigenvalue of the transfer matrix (2.14) is $\lambda=0$ , which implies that the corresponding eigenvectors obey

$$ \mathbb{T}|r)=(l|\mathbb{T}=0\,,\qquad(l|r)=1\,, $$

and we furthermore restrict $V_{\pm\infty}$ such that the conditions (2.19) are satisfied. These conditions ensure that the RCMPS is normalized.

### 2.3 Matrix notation and RCMPS gauge redundancy

To further characterize the zero-eigenvectors $(l|$ and $|r)$ , it is convenient to interpret these eigenvectors as $\chi\times\chi$ matrices. Such an identification is possible because the matrix $\mathbb{T}$ acts (on the right) on vectors $|u)\in\mathbb{C}^{\chi}\otimes\overline{\mathbb{C}}^{\chi}$ and on the left on co-vectors $(w|\in\overline{\mathbb{C}}^{\chi}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{\chi}$ . From the components of $|u)$ and $(w|$ we can build the components $u_{i}{}^{j}$ and $w_{i}{}^{j}$ of the matrices $u$ and $w$ using the standard rule for Kronecker products

$$ |u)_{(i-1)\chi+j}\ \cong\ u_{i}{}^{j}\,,\qquad(w|_{(i-1)\chi+j}\ \cong\ [w^{\dagger}]_{j}{}^{i}\,,\qquad i,j=1,\ldots,\chi\,. $$

In this notation, the inner product and the action of an operator of the form $A\otimes B$ become

$$ \begin{split}(w|u)\ &\cong\ \tr(w^{\dagger}u)\,,\\
[A\otimes\overline{B}|u)]_{(i-1)\chi+j}\ &\cong\ [AuB^{\dagger}]_{i}{}^{j}\,,\\
[(w|A\otimes\overline{B}]_{(i-1)\chi+j}\ &\cong\ [B^{\dagger}w^{\dagger}A]_{j}{}^{i}\,.\end{split} $$

We can then write the eigenvalue equations (2.20) as

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{T}|r) \displaystyle=0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad Qr+rQ^{\dagger}+RrR^{\dagger}=0\,, \displaystyle(l|\mathbb{T} \displaystyle=0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad Q^{\dagger}l+lQ+R^{\dagger}lR=0\,. $$

The structure of the transfer matrix (2.23) furthermore guarantees that the fixed points $r$ and $l$ are positive definite matrices [31] and, in particular, Hermitian.

The RCMPS ansatz is overparameterized in the sense that the transformation

$$ Q\rightarrow XQX^{-1}\,,\qquad R\rightarrow XRX^{-1} $$

does not change the physical state for any invertible matrix $X$ .77 7 From the definition (2.10), it is clear that this gauge transformation should be accompanied by a transformation of the boundary vectors $V_{\pm\infty}$ for the state to be invariant. However, since the boundary vectors do not change bulk observables, we can safely ignore their transformation. We can use this redundancy to trivialize the left or right fixed point [31] i.e. set $l=\mathds{1}$ or $r=\mathds{1}$ , respectively. In this work, we will do the former and use

$$ \text{{left-gauge}:}\qquad l=\mathds{1}\,, $$

which implies that the right fixed point satisfies $\tr(r)=1$ , as per the normalization condition $(l|r)=\tr(lr)=1$ . The choice $l=\mathds{1}$ further constrains the matrices $Q,R$ through (2.23)

$$ Q^{\dagger}+Q+R^{\dagger}R=0\,, $$

which fixes the Hermitian part of $Q$ in terms of $R^{\dagger}R$ .

### 2.4 Generating functional for correlators of $a(x)$ and $a^{\dagger}(x)$

Having defined the states $|Q,R\rangle$ , we would now like to compute expectation values of various (normal-ordered) operators in these states, most importantly of the Hamiltonian density ${\cal H}$ . All normal-ordered operators can be written in terms of normal-ordered products of $a(x)$ and $a^{\dagger}(x)$ , so the first step is to compute a generating functional for such products:

$$ \mathcal{Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]\equiv\left\langle Q,R\middle|N_{\mu}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\left(\tilde{\jmath}(x)a^{\dagger}(x)+j(x)a(x)\right)}\right]\middle|Q,R\right\rangle\,, $$

where $\tilde{\jmath}$ and $j$ are classical sources, which, for simplicity, we assume to have compact support. Since

$$ N_{\mu}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\left(\tilde{\jmath}(x)a^{\dagger}(x)+j(x)a(x)\right)}\right]=e^{-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\tilde{\jmath}(x)j(x)}e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,j(x)a(x)}e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\tilde{\jmath}(x)a^{\dagger}(x)}\,, $$

we can relate (2.27) to the overlap of two generalized RCMPSs that were defined in (2.11):

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j] \displaystyle=e^{-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\tilde{\jmath}(x)j(x)}\langle{\bf Q}^{\prime},{\bf R}^{\prime}|{\bf Q},{\bf R}\rangle\,, $$

with ${\bf Q}^{\prime}(x)={\bf Q}(x)=Q$ , ${\bf R}^{\prime}(x)=R+\overline{j}(x)\mathds{1}$ , and ${\bf R}(x)=R+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}$ , and with identical boundary vectors at both ends, $V_{\pm\infty}^{\prime}=V_{\pm\infty}$ . Now the expression for the generating functional follows directly from (2.12):

$$ \mathcal{Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]=\left(v_{+\infty}\middle|\mathcal{P}\exp\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,[\mathbb{T}+j(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}]\right)\middle|v_{-\infty}\right)\,, $$

where we used the definitions (2.14) and where the $\tilde{\jmath}j$ arising from product of $\mathbf{R}$ s in (2.12) cancels against the prefactor in (2.29).

We are now in a position to understand why the precise choice of boundary vectors $V_{\pm\infty}$ does not affect the bulk observables computed from the generating functional (2.30). Any observable of interest can be derived from $\mathcal{Z}$ using functions $j$ and $\tilde{\jmath}$ that have compact support, or that vanish sufficiently fast at infinity. Suppose both $j$ and $\tilde{\jmath}$ vanish outside some interval $[x_{1},x_{2}]$ . We can then split the path-ordered exponential in (2.30) into three factors, corresponding to the intervals $(-\infty,x_{1}]$ , $[x_{1},x_{2}]$ , and $[x_{2},\infty]$ , where for the former and latter we can use (2.17):

$$ \begin{split}&\mathcal{P}\exp\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,[\mathbb{T}+j(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}]\right)\\
&\qquad\qquad=\left|r\middle)\middle(l\middle|\mathcal{P}\exp\left(\int_{x_{1}}^{x_{2}}dx\,[\mathbb{T}+j(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}]\right)\middle|r\middle)\middle(l\right|\,.\end{split} $$

In this expression, one can use (2.17) to further extend the integration limits on the RHS to the entire real line. Using the normalization condition (2.18), we arrive at

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]=\left(l\middle|\mathcal{P}\exp\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,[\mathbb{T}+j(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}]\right)\middle|r\right)\,, $$

which is manifestly independent of the choice of boundary vectors. It follows that the precise choices of these vectors do not affect any bulk observables. Note that the expression (2.32) was derived for sources $j,\tilde{\jmath}$ with compact support, but the precise interval $[x_{1},x_{2}]$ on which these functions are supported does not enter in the final answer. It can be shown that (2.32) continues to hold even if $j,\tilde{\jmath}$ do not have compact support but instead decay at $\pm\infty$ sufficiently fast.

The expression (2.32) is the final answer for the generating functional, but it is still onerous to evaluate it as written. An efficient strategy is to recast ${\cal Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]$ as the solution to a differential equation. In particular, define the vector

$$ \bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)\equiv\left.\mathcal{P}\exp\left(\int_{-\infty}^{x}dy\,[\mathbb{T}+j(y)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(y)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}]\right)\middle|r\right)\,, $$

in terms of which the generating functional is simply

$$ \mathcal{Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]=\bigl(l\big|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(\infty)\bigr)\,. $$

The advantage of defining (2.33) is that $\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)$ obeys the differential equation

$$ \frac{d\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)}{dx}=[\mathbb{T}+j(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}]\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)\,,\qquad\text{with }\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(-\infty)\bigr)=|r)\,. $$

For given source functions $j,\tilde{\jmath}$ , this is just a system of $\chi^{2}$ ODEs that can be solved numerically.

Note that if $j,\tilde{\jmath}$ are compactly supported on the interval $[x_{1},x_{2}]$ , then outside of this interval, the differential equation (2.35) takes the form

$$ \frac{d\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)}{dx}=\mathbb{T}\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)\,,\qquad\text{for $x<x_{1}$ or $x>x_{2}$}\,. $$

In terms of the right-eigenvectors $|r_{k})$ of $\mathbb{T}$ (with $|r_{1})=|r)$ ), the general solution of the equation (2.36) is

$$ \bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)=c_{1}|r)+\sum_{k>1}c_{k}e^{\lambda_{k}x}|r_{k})\,,\qquad\text{for $x<x_{1}$ or $x>x_{2}$}\,, $$

for some constants $c_{k}$ . (We have a different set of $c_{k}$ for $x<x_{1}$ and $x>x_{2}$ .) Since $\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits\lambda_{k}<0$ for all $k>1$ , the exponentials in (2.37) all grow as $x\to-\infty$ , and thus the boundary condition $\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(-\infty)\bigr)=|r)$ means that $\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)=|r)$ for all $x<x_{1}$ . It follows that we can start solving the differential equation (2.35) at $x=x_{1}$ . For $x>x_{2}$ , the exponentials in (2.37) all decay as $x\to\infty$ , and thus the solution approaches $c_{1}|r)$ exponentially fast. Thus, a good approximation can be obtained by solving the differential equation (2.35) on a finite interval $[-L,L]$ instead of the entire real line.

Alternatively, one can also integrate from $+\infty$ to $-\infty$ instead. Indeed, one can define the co-vector

$$ \bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr|\equiv\left(l\middle|\mathcal{P}\exp\left(\int_{x}^{\infty}dy\,[\mathbb{T}+j(y)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(y)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}]\right)\right.\,, $$

in terms of which the generating functional is

$$ \mathcal{Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]=\bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(-\infty)\big|r\bigr)\,. $$

The vector (2.38) obeys the differential equation

$$ \frac{d\bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr|}{dx}=-\bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr|[\mathbb{T}+j(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}]\,,\qquad\text{with }\bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(\infty)\bigr|=(l|\,. $$

This is again a system of $\chi^{2}$ ODEs that can be solved numerically.

### 2.5 Expectation values in RCMPS

Let us now move on to the expectation values of operators of interest, which are the Hamiltonian density (2.6) and potentially powers of the field operator $\phi$ . We will primarily compute the expectation values of three types of operators: the Hamiltonian density ${\cal H}_{\text{free}}(x)$ of a free scalar field of the same mass $\mu$ as the mass parameter used for normal ordering, a vertex operator $V_{b}$ with parameter $b$ , and powers of $\phi$ :

$$ \begin{split}{\cal H}_{\text{free}}(x)&\equiv N_{\mu}\left[\frac{1}{2}\pi^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}\phi^{2}\right]\,,\\
V_{b}(x)&\equiv N_{\mu}\left[e^{b\phi(x)}\right]\,,\\
{\cal O}_{n}(x)&\equiv N_{\mu}\left[\phi(x)^{n}\right]\,.\end{split} $$

These operators will serve as building blocks for all local operators that we will be interested in. For instance, for the two examples mentioned in (2.3), the Hamiltonian density is

$$ \begin{split}\text{$\phi^{4}$ theory:}&\qquad{\cal H}_{\phi^{4}}={\cal H}_{\text{free}}+\frac{1}{2}(m^{2}-\mu^{2}){\cal O}_{2}+g{\cal O}_{4}\,,\\
\text{sine-Gordon theory:}&\qquad{\cal H}_{\text{sG}}={\cal H}_{\text{free}}-\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}{\cal O}_{2}-\frac{m^{2}}{2\beta^{2}}(V_{i\beta}+V_{-i\beta})+\frac{m^{2}}{\beta^{2}}\,.\end{split} $$

To compute the expectation values of the operators (2.41), we should express $\phi(x)$ and $\pi(x)$ in terms of $a(x),a^{\dagger}(x)$ by combining the definitions (2.5) and (2.7). For $\phi(x)$ , this relation is

$$ \begin{split}\phi(x)&=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dy\,J(x-y)\left[a(y)+a^{\dagger}(y)\right]\,,\end{split} $$

where we defined the kernel

$$ J(x)\equiv\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk}{2\pi}\frac{e^{ikx}}{\sqrt{2\omega_{k}}}=\frac{\mu^{1/4}}{2^{1/4}\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma(\frac{1}{4})}\frac{K_{1/4}(\mu|x|)}{|x|^{1/4}}\,. $$

(We will not need the analogous relation for $\pi(x)$ .) Note that the function $J(x)$ has an integrable singularity at $x=0$ and decays as $\sim\frac{e^{-\mu|x|}}{(\mu|x|)^{3/4}}$ for $|x|\gg\mu^{-1}$ . The non-locality of the relation (2.43) makes computations using RCMPSs more involved than those using their non-relativistic counterparts, where the field operators are fully local. Note that due to translation invariance of the RCMPS, the expectation values of the operators in (2.41) are $x$ -independent, so we can set $x=0$ .

One notable feature of RCMPSs is that they encode the expected UV behavior of two-point functions. To see this, we note that expectation values in the RCMPS ansatz (2.10) of normal-ordered operators are finite as they can be evaluated using the generating function (2.32). In particular, this implies that the two-point function of $\phi(x)$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\langle Q,R|\phi(x)\phi(y)|Q,R\rangle \displaystyle=G_{\mu}(x-y)+\langle Q,R|N_{\mu}[\phi(x)\phi(y)]|Q,R\rangle \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{4\pi}\log\left[\mu^{2}(x-y)^{2}\right]+\text{regular terms}\,, $$

where the singular behavior derives from the free equal-time two-point function $G_{\mu}(x-y)=\langle 0|\phi(x)\phi(y)|0\rangle$ . This singular behavior is exactly what is expected for the interacting theory (2.6), because all interactions are relevant and, accordingly, the theory is free in the UV.

#### 2.5.1 Expectation value of the vertex operator $V_{b}$

Of the operators in (2.41), the simplest expectation value is that of $V_{b}$ because using (2.43) we see that

$$ \left\langle Q,R\middle|V_{b}(0)\middle|Q,R\right\rangle={\cal Z}[bJ,bJ]\,, $$

with ${\cal Z}$ being the generating functional defined in (2.27) that we computed in the previous section. The expectation value (2.46) can be computed either from (2.34) or from (2.39) after solving numerically the differential equations (2.35) or (2.40), respectively, in the particular case $j=\tilde{\jmath}=bJ$ . Due to the fact that the kernel $J(x)$ decays exponentially at large distances, one can obtain a good approximation by solving the differential equation on the interval $[-L,L]$ for a sufficiently large $L$ —see the discussion after (2.35).

#### 2.5.2 Expectation value of ${\cal O}_{n}$

We now turn to the expectation values of the normal-ordered monomials ${\cal O}_{n}=N_{\mu}[\phi^{n}(x)]$ . As explained in [1], the most efficient way of computing $\langle{\cal O}_{n}(x)\rangle$ is to use $\langle V_{b}\rangle$ as a generating function for monomials:

$$ \langle Q,R|{\cal O}_{n}(x)|Q,R\rangle=\left.\frac{\partial^{n}}{\partial b^{n}}\langle Q,R|V_{b}(x)|Q,R\rangle\right|_{b=0}\,. $$

As for $V_{b}(0)$ itself, we evaluate the expectation value of ${\cal O}_{n}(0)$ using ODEs. These ODEs can be obtained by taking $n$ derivatives with respect to $b$ of the equations (2.33)–(2.40), with $j=\tilde{\jmath}=bJ$ , and then setting $b=0$ .

Thus, we define the $n$ th derivative of $|r_{bJ,bJ}(x))$

$$ |r^{(n)}(x))\equiv\left.\frac{\partial^{n}|r_{bJ,bJ}(x))}{\partial b^{n}}\right|_{b=0}\,, $$

which, from (2.34) and (2.46), allows us to write

$$ \langle Q,R|{\cal O}_{n}(0)|Q,R\rangle=\bigl(l\big|r^{(n)}(\infty)\bigr)\,. $$

Note that $\big|r^{(0)}(x)\bigr)=|r)$ is $x$ -independent. In practice, the vectors $\bigl|r^{(n)}(x)\bigr)$ , with $n>0$ , can be computed efficiently by solving a separate system of ODEs derived from (2.35) by repeated differentiation:

$$ \frac{d\bigl|r^{(n)}(x)\bigr)}{dx}=\mathbb{T}\bigl|r^{(n)}(x))+nJ(x)(R\otimes\mathds{1}+\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R})|r^{(n-1)}(x)\bigr)\,, $$

with the boundary condition

$$ \bigl|r^{(n)}(-\infty)\bigr)=0\qquad\text{for $n>0$}\,. $$

To compute $\bigl|r^{(n)}(x)\bigr)$ , one has to solve the equations for $\bigl|r^{(n^{\prime})}(x)\bigr)$ with all $1\leq n^{\prime}\leq n$ .

One can also derive an analogous system of ODEs using $\bigl(l_{bJ,bJ}(x)\bigr|$ by taking derivatives of (2.39) and (2.40). In particular, we have

$$ \langle Q,R|{\cal O}_{n}(0)|Q,R\rangle=\bigl(l^{(n)}(-\infty)\big|r\bigr)\,, $$

where

$$ (l^{(n)}(x)|\equiv\left.\frac{\partial^{n}(l_{bJ,bJ}(x)|}{\partial b^{n}}\right|_{b=0}\,, $$

with $(l^{(0)}|=(l|$ , and $(l^{(n)}(x)|$ with $n>0$ obeys

$$ \frac{d\bigl(l^{(n)}(x)\bigr|}{dx}=-\bigl(l^{(n)}(x)\bigr|\mathbb{T}-nJ(x)\bigl(l^{(n-1)}(x)\bigr|\left(R\otimes\mathds{1}+\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\right)\,,\qquad\text{with }\bigl(l^{(n)}(\infty)\bigr|=0\,. $$

This method of evaluating VEVs of ${\cal O}_{n}$ by solving a system of ODEs rather than by performing a large number of iterated integrals is one of the main technical insights of [1]. We will adapt this method to the RQP ansatz in the following section.

#### 2.5.3 Expectation value of ${\cal H}_{\text{free}}$

Lastly, let us now discuss the computation of the normal ordered free Hamiltonian density ${\cal H}_{\text{free}}$ defined in (2.41). Writing the operators $\phi$ and $\pi$ in terms of the creation and annihilation operators $a_{k}$ and $a_{k}^{\dagger}$ , it is straightforward to show that in any translation-invariant state we have

$$ \langle\mathcal{H}_{\text{free}}(0)\rangle=\int\frac{dk\,dk^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\frac{(\mu+ik)(\mu-ik^{\prime})}{\sqrt{\omega_{k}\omega_{k^{\prime}}}}\langle a_{k^{\prime}}^{\dagger}a_{k}\rangle\,. $$

(See Appendix A.2 for a detailed proof.) Using the definitions (2.7), this expression can be written in terms of $a(x)$ and $a^{\dagger}(x)$ :

$$ \langle{\cal H}_{\text{free}}(0)\rangle=2\int dy\,dz\,H(y)H(z)\langle a^{\dagger}(y)a(z)\rangle\,,\qquad H(x)\equiv(\mu-\partial_{x})J(x)\,. $$

In an RCMPS $|Q,R\rangle$ , the expression (2.56) implies that the expectation value of ${\cal H}_{\text{free}}(0)$ can be written in terms of the generating functional (2.27) as

$$ \langle Q,R|{\cal H}_{\text{free}}(0)|Q,R\rangle=2\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\alpha\partial\beta}{\cal Z}[\alpha H,\beta H]\bigg|_{\alpha=\beta=0}\,. $$

Note that this approach for computing $\langle{\cal H}_{\text{free}}(0)\rangle$ differs from that presented in [1] and requires one to solve only half the number of ODEs. The generating functional ${\cal Z}[\alpha H,\beta H]$ can be computed from (2.34) by solving (2.35) with $j=\beta H$ and $\tilde{\jmath}=\alpha H$ . However, this differential equation is complicated to solve because $H(x)\sim 1/|x|^{3/2}$ at small $x$ , which is not a classically integrable singularity and would have to be treated as a distribution. Since the $1/|x|^{3/2}$ behavior of $H(x)$ comes solely from terms involving derivatives of $J(x)$ , it is possible to get rid of these derivatives (and hence of the non-integrable divergence) by making the definition

$$ \bigl|r_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr)=e^{-F(x)}\bigl|\tilde{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr)\,,\qquad F(x)\equiv\beta J(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\alpha J(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\,, $$

where $e^{-F}$ is an integrating factor. Using (2.35), one can then show that the quantity $\bigl|\tilde{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr)$ obeys the differential equation

$$ \frac{d\bigl|\tilde{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr)}{dx}=e^{F(x)}\bigl(\mathbb{T}+\beta\mu J(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\alpha\mu J(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\bigr)e^{-F(x)}\bigl|\tilde{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr)\,, $$

with the boundary condition $\bigl|\tilde{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(-\infty)\bigr)=|r)$ that follows from (2.35) and the fact that $F\to 0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ . That $F$ vanishes at infinity also implies

$$ {\cal Z}[\alpha H,\beta H]=(l|\tilde{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(\infty))\,. $$

Note that the differential equation (2.59) involves only $J(x)$ , which has an integrable singularity at $x=0$ , and it is therefore simpler to solve than (2.35).

We can now go back to (2.57), and, using (2.60), write the expectation value of the free Hamiltonian as

$$ \langle Q,R|{\cal H}_{\text{free}}(0)|Q,R\rangle=2\bigl(l\big|\tilde{r}^{(1,1)}(\infty)\bigr)\,, $$

where we defined

$$ \big|\tilde{r}^{(n,m)}(x)\big)\equiv\left.\frac{\partial^{n+m}|\tilde{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x))}{\partial\alpha^{n}\partial\beta^{m}}\right|_{\alpha=\beta=0}\,. $$

Note that $\big|\tilde{r}^{(0,0)}(x)\big)=|r)$ . By taking derivatives of (2.59), we obtain a system of equations for $\big|\tilde{r}^{(n,m)}(x)\bigr)$ with $n,m\leq 1$ :

$$ \begin{split}\frac{d\bigl|\tilde{r}^{(1,1)}(x)\bigr)}{dx}&=\mathbb{T}\bigl|\tilde{r}^{(1,1)}(x)\bigr)+J(x)\left(\mu R+[R,Q]\right)\otimes\mathds{1}\bigl|\tilde{r}^{(1,0)}(x)\bigr)\\
&{}+J(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\left(\mu\overline{R}+[\overline{R},\overline{Q}]\right)\bigl|\tilde{r}^{(0,1)}(x)\bigr)\,,\\
\frac{d\bigl|\tilde{r}^{(1,0)}(x)\bigr)}{dx}&=\mathbb{T}\bigl|\tilde{r}^{(1,0)}(x)\bigr)+J(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\left(\mu\overline{R}+[\overline{R},\overline{Q}]\right)\bigl|r\bigr)\,,\\
\frac{d\bigl|\tilde{r}^{(0,1)}(x)\bigr)}{dx}&=\mathbb{T}\bigl|\tilde{r}^{(0,1)}(x)\bigr)+J(x)\left(\mu R+[R,Q]\right)\otimes\mathds{1}\bigl|r\bigr)\,,\end{split} $$

with the boundary conditions $\bigl|\tilde{r}^{(m,n)}(-\infty)\bigr)=0$ for $(m,n)\neq(0,0)$ . The system of equations (2.63) can be solved simultaneously, and from the solution we can then determine $\langle Q,R|{\cal H}_{\text{free}}(0)|Q,R\rangle$ via (2.61).

Finally, following (2.39), we can repeat this procedure while integrating in the other direction by considering $\big(\tilde{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}\big|$ defined through

$$ \bigl(l_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr|=\bigl(\tilde{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr|e^{F(x)}\,. $$

One can then utilize (2.40) to find

$$ \frac{d\bigl(\tilde{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr|}{dx}=-\bigl(\tilde{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr|e^{F(x)}\bigl(\mathbb{T}+\beta\mu J(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\alpha\mu J(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\bigr)e^{-F(x)}\,. $$

With this, the expectation value of the free Hamiltonian density takes the form

$$ \langle Q,R|{\cal H}_{\text{free}}(0)|Q,R\rangle=2\big(\tilde{l}^{(1,1)}(-\infty)\big|r\big)\,, $$

where

$$ \big(\tilde{l}^{(n,m)}(x)\big|\equiv\left.\frac{\partial^{n+m}\big(\tilde{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\big|}{\partial\alpha^{n}\partial\beta^{m}}\right|_{\alpha=\beta=0}\,. $$

The system of differential equations needed to be solved is

$$ \begin{split}\frac{d\bigl(\tilde{l}^{(1,1)}(x)\bigr|}{dx}&=-\bigl(\tilde{l}^{(1,1)}(x)\bigr|\mathbb{T}-J(x)\bigl(\tilde{l}^{(1,0)}(x)\bigr|\left(\mu R+[R,Q]\right)\otimes\mathds{1}\\
&{}-J(x)\bigl(\tilde{l}^{(0,1)}(x)\bigr|\mathds{1}\otimes\left(\mu\overline{R}+[\overline{R},\overline{Q}]\right)\,,\\
\frac{d\bigl(\tilde{l}^{(1,0)}(x)\bigr|}{dx}&=-\bigl(\tilde{l}^{(1,0)}(x)\bigr|\mathbb{T}-J(x)\bigl(l\bigr|\mathds{1}\otimes\left(\mu\overline{R}+[\overline{R},\overline{Q}]\right)\,,\\
\frac{d\bigl(\tilde{l}^{(0,1)}(x)\bigr|}{dx}&=-\bigl(\tilde{l}^{(0,1)}(x)\bigr|\mathbb{T}-J(x)\bigl(l\bigr|\left(\mu R+[R,Q]\right)\otimes\mathds{1}\,,\end{split} $$

accompanied by the boundary conditions $\big(\tilde{l}^{(n,m)}(\infty)\big|=0$ for $(n,m)\neq(0,0)$ .

## 3 Relativistic Quasiparticle ansatz

We will now define the RQP ansatz and derive the formulas needed to determine the spectrum of excitations. As explained in Section 2.1, RCMPSs differ from CMPSs only in that the physical operators of interest are non-local when written in terms of the operators $a(x)$ appearing in the ansatz. Thus, we can straightforwardly adapt the CMPS quasiparticle ansatz [23] to the RCMPS framework. For simplicity, in this section we will first focus on particle-like excitations and postpone the generalizations to solitonic excitations to Section 3.6.

### 3.1 Definition of the RQP ansatz

The RQP ansatz is a state that resembles the vacuum state $|Q,R\rangle$ for $|x|\rightarrow\infty$ , with a local perturbation at a position $x$ parameterized by two $\chi\times\chi$ matrices $V,W$ , further smeared into a plane wave of momentum $k$ :

$$ \displaystyle|V,W;k\rangle \displaystyle\equiv\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,e^{ikx}V_{+\infty}^{\dagger}\mathcal{P}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dy\,\left(Q\otimes\mathds{1}+R\otimes a^{\dagger}(y)\right)}\left(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes a^{\dagger}(x)\right)\right]V_{-\infty}|0\rangle\,. $$

Here, the path ordering refers to everything inside the square bracket, so it can also be written as a path ordered exponential from $x$ to $\infty$ , $\mathcal{P}e^{\int_{x}^{\infty}dy\,\left(Q\otimes\mathds{1}+R\otimes a^{\dagger}(y)\right)}$ , followed by the factor $\left(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes a^{\dagger}(x)\right)$ , followed by a path ordered exponential from $-\infty$ to $x$ , $\mathcal{P}e^{\int_{-\infty}^{x}dy\,\left(Q\otimes\mathds{1}+R\otimes a^{\dagger}(y)\right)}$ . Also note that the spatial profile of the RQP is not that of a delta function because the local perturbation can influence a finite neighborhood around $x$ through the virtual indices of $V,W$ .

It is useful to view the state $|V,W;k\rangle$ above as a linearized variation of the generalized RCMPS $|{\bf Q},{\bf R}\rangle$ defined in (2.11), expanded around the state $|Q,R\rangle$ , with a specific plane-wave profile for $\delta\mathbf{Q}$ and $\delta\mathbf{R}$ :

$$ |V,W;k\rangle=\delta|\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{R}\rangle\Big|_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{Q}(x)=Q\\
\mathbf{R}(x)=R\end{subarray}}\qquad\text{with}\qquad\begin{aligned} \delta\mathbf{Q}(x)&=e^{ikx}V\,,\\
\delta\mathbf{R}(x)&=e^{ikx}W\,.\end{aligned} $$

All properties of the RQP states $|V,W;k\rangle$ can thus be derived from the properties of the generalized RCMPSs $|{\bf Q},{\bf R}\rangle$ by taking a variation as in (3.2).

The first requirement we should impose is that the states $|V,W;k\rangle$ should be orthogonal to the RCMPS $|Q,R\rangle$ . The inner product $\langle Q,R|V,W;k\rangle$ can be computed as the variation of the inner product (2.12) of two generalized RCMPSs, where we only vary the ket $|{\bf Q},{\bf R}\rangle$ , and afterwards we set ${\bf Q}^{\prime}={\bf Q}=Q$ , ${\bf R}^{\prime}={\bf R}=R$ , and $V_{\pm}^{\prime}=V_{\pm}$ . The result can be written as

$$ \langle Q,R|V,W;k\rangle=\int dx\,e^{ikx}\left(v_{+\infty}\middle|e^{\int_{x}^{\infty}dy\,\mathbb{T}}\left(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R}\right)e^{\int_{-\infty}^{x}dy\,\mathbb{T}}\middle|v_{-\infty}\right)\,. $$

Further, using the normalization conditions (2.19) of the RCMPS and the fact that the exponential of the $\mathbb{T}$ matrix with a large coefficient amounts to a projection operator, as in (2.17), one can simplify the inner product above to

$$ \langle Q,R|V,W;k\rangle=2\pi\delta(k)\left(l|V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R}|r\right)\,. $$

As expected, RQP states with non-zero momentum are orthogonal to the (zero-momentum) RCMPS $|Q,R\rangle$ , but this is not necessarily the case for $k=0$ . Thus, we restrict the RQP with any $k$ to be orthogonal to the RCMPS by requiring $V,W$ to obey

$$ \left(l\middle|(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R})\middle|r\right)=0\,. $$

A similar calculation gives the inner product of two RQP excitations over the same $|Q,R\rangle$ RCMPS:

$$ \displaystyle\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k^{\prime}|V,W;k\rangle \displaystyle=2\pi\delta(k-k^{\prime})\Biggl[\,\left(l\middle|\,W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\,\middle|r\right) \displaystyle{}+\left(l\middle|\left(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{V}^{\prime}+R\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\right)\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}d\xi\,e^{(\mathbb{T}-ik)\xi}\right)\left(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R}\right)\middle|r\right) \displaystyle{}+\left(l\middle|\left(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R}\right)\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}d\xi\,e^{(\mathbb{T}+ik)\xi}\right)\left(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{V}^{\prime}+R\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\right)\middle|r\right)\Biggr]\,. $$

The second and third lines of this expression can be made to vanish by an appropriate choice of gauge. In particular, the RQP ansatz (3.1) introduces its own redundancy

$$ V\rightarrow V+[X,Q]+ikX\,,\qquad W\rightarrow W+[X,R]\,, $$

which is the analog of (2.24). Under (3.7), the integrand in (3.1) changes by a total derivative. Combined with the choice (3.5), we will use this freedom to set

$$ \text{{tangent left-gauge}:}\qquad(l|(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R})=0\,, $$

which we refer to as tangent left-gauge.88 8 The name tangent is appropriate as the RQP ansatz (3.1) can be interpreted as a “boosted” tangent vector to the RCMPS manifold. We use the term tangent left gauge as opposed to simply left gauge because the latter refers to the gauge choice made for the base RCMPS.,99 9 Alternatively, we can use the gauge freedom to set $\left(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R}\right)|r)=0$ , which corresponds to tangent right-gauge. In tangent left-gauge, the inner product between two RQP states is

$$ \begin{split}\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k^{\prime}|V,W;k\rangle&=2\pi\delta(k-k^{\prime})\,\left(l\middle|\,W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\,\middle|r\right)\,.\end{split} $$

In the matrix notation introduced, the tangent left-gauge condition reads $V^{\dagger}l+W^{\dagger}lR=0$ , which allows us to solve for $V$ :

$$ \text{{tangent left-gauge}:}\qquad V=-l^{-1}R^{\dagger}lW\,. $$

In all subsequent equations, the tangent left-gauge should be assumed (unless stated otherwise) and all occurrences of $V$ should be understood as $V=-l^{-1}R^{\dagger}lW$ . In the tangent left-gauge, the inner product of two RQP states in (3.9) reads

$$ \langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k^{\prime}|V,W;k\rangle=2\pi\delta(k-k^{\prime})\tr(W^{\prime\dagger}lWr)\,. $$

### 3.2 Computing the excitation energy

To estimate the spectrum, we apply the Rayleigh-Ritz method to restrict the Hamiltonian to the basis of RQP $|V,W;k\rangle$ over the RCMPS $|Q,R\rangle$ . Thus, we consider the projected time-independent Schrödinger equation

$$ \langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k^{\prime}|H|V,W;k\rangle=\left(\omega(k)+E_{\text{RCMPS}}\right)\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k^{\prime}|V,W;k\rangle\,, $$

where $\omega(k)$ is the excitation energy of the RQP and $E_{\text{RCMPS}}\equiv\langle Q,R|H|Q,R\rangle$ is the (formally infinite) energy of the RCMPS, which we can also write as

$$ E_{\text{RCMPS}}=\langle Q,R|{\cal H}(0)|Q,R\rangle\,\frac{\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k|V,W;k\rangle}{\left(l\middle|\,W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\,\middle|r\right)}\,, $$

where ${\cal H}(x)$ is the Hamiltonian density. The inner product on the RHS of (3.12) was already evaluated in (3.9). For the LHS, we write $H=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,{\cal H}(x)$ and use the fact that ${\cal H}(x)=e^{-iPx}{\cal H}(0)e^{iPx}$ together with $P|V,W;k\rangle=k|V,W;k\rangle$ , where $P$ is the momentum operator,1010 10 We can write $P=\int\frac{dk}{2\pi}ka_{k}^{\dagger}a_{k}$ , as usual, even though $a_{k}$ and $a_{k}^{\dagger}$ are the ladder operators corresponding to only the free part of the Hamiltonian. to simplify (3.12) to

$$ 2\pi\delta(k-k^{\prime})\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k^{\prime}|\mathcal{H}(0)|V,W;k\rangle=2\pi\delta(k-k^{\prime})\left(\omega(k)+E_{\text{RCMPS}}\right)\left(l\middle|\,W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\,\middle|r\right)\,. $$

As RCMPSs are cluster-decomposing, the matrix element of a local operator such as the Hamiltonian density decomposes into a connected and disconnected contribution

$$ \langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k^{\prime}|\mathcal{H}(0)|V,W;k\rangle=\langle Q,R|\mathcal{H}(0)|Q,R\rangle\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k^{\prime}|V,W;k\rangle+\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k^{\prime}|\mathcal{H}(0)|V,W;k\rangle_{\text{conn}}\,, $$

where the disconnected piece contains a delta function (see (3.9)) and the connected piece is regular as $k^{\prime}\to k$ . Plugging (3.15) and (3.13) into (3.14), we notice that the disconnected piece of (3.15) precisely cancels the $E_{\text{RCMPS}}$ term on the RHS, giving

$$ 2\pi\delta(k-k^{\prime})\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k^{\prime}|\mathcal{H}(0)|V,W;k\rangle_{\text{conn}}=2\pi\delta(k-k^{\prime})\omega(k)\left(l\middle|\,W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\,\middle|r\right)\,. $$

We can then cancel the delta functions from both sides of this equation and set $k^{\prime}=k$ in the remaining expression. Accordingly, the eigenvalue problem is

$$ \langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k|\mathcal{H}(0)|V,W;k\rangle_{\text{conn}}=\omega(k)\left(l\middle|\,W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\,\middle|r\right)\,. $$

The LHS of (3.17) determines the matrix elements of an effective Hamiltonian $H_{\text{eff}}$ that acts linearly on the space of matrices $W$ , defined implicitly by

$$ \tr(W^{\prime\dagger}lH_{\text{eff},k}(W)r)\equiv\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k|\mathcal{H}(0)|V,W;k\rangle_{\text{conn}}\,, $$

As determining the connected part of the matrix element is a linear operation, we can compute the effective RQP Hamiltonian for each term appearing in the Hamiltonian individually. For the operators (2.41), we define the effective operators

$$ \begin{split}\tr\left[W^{\prime\dagger}l{\mathbf{H}}_{k}(W)r\right]&\equiv\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k|\mathcal{H}_{\text{free}}(0)|V,W;k\rangle_{\text{conn}}\\
\tr\left[W^{\prime\dagger}l{\bf{V}}_{b,k}(W)r\right]&\equiv\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k|V_{b}(0)|V,W;k\rangle_{\text{conn}}\\
\tr\left[W^{\prime\dagger}l{\bf{O}}_{n,k}(W)r\right]&\equiv\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k|\mathcal{O}_{n}(0)|V,W;k\rangle_{\text{conn}}\end{split} $$

Then the full effective Hamiltonians take the form

$$ \begin{split}\text{$\phi^{4}$ theory:}&\qquad{H}^{\phi^{4}}_{\text{eff},k}(W)=\mathbf{H}_{k}(W)+\frac{1}{2}(m^{2}-\mu^{2})\,\mathbf{O}_{2,k}(W)+g\,\mathbf{O}_{4,k}(W)\,,\\
\text{sine-Gordon:}&\qquad{H}^{\text{sG}}_{\text{eff},k}(W)=\mathbf{H}_{k}(W)-\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}\,\mathbf{O}_{2,k}(W)-\frac{m^{2}}{2\beta^{2}}\left(\mathbf{V}_{i\beta,k}(W)+\mathbf{V}_{-i\beta,k}(W)\right)\,.\end{split} $$

Given the effective Hamiltonian, the dispersion relation $\omega(k)$ of the RQP ansatz can then be extracted by solving the eigenvalue problem1111 11 In the tangent left-gauge, this is more naturally a generalized eigenvalue problem as one has a non-trivial metric as implemented by the multiplication of $l$ and $r$ in (3.9). In (3.21), this metric has been removed by inverting $l$ and $r$ when defining (3.18). involving finite matrices

$$ H_{\text{eff},k}(W)=\omega(k)W\,. $$

One can determine up to $\chi^{2}$ eigenvalues from (3.21), but typically only the lowest eigenvalues can be interpreted as asymptotic states. Most eigenvalues of (3.21) will fall in the two-particle continuum, and such two-body states are poorly approximated by the RQP ansatz (3.1) and thus the associated energies should not be trusted.

### 3.3 Generating functional for matrix elements of $a(x)$ and $a^{\dagger}(x)$

To compute matrix elements of local operators in the RQP states, let us define the generating functional for matrix elements of products of $a(x)$ and $a^{\dagger}(x)$ :

$$ \widetilde{\cal Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]\equiv\left\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k^{\prime}\middle|N_{\mu}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\left(\tilde{\jmath}(x)a^{\dagger}(x)+j(x)a(x)\right)}\right]\middle|V,W;k\right\rangle\,. $$

As in Section 2.4, we assume that the source functions $j(x)$ and $\tilde{\jmath}(x)$ are of compact support. Given the interpretation of the RQP states as variations of generalized RCMPSs, as in (3.2), the expression (3.22) can be recast as

$$ \widetilde{\cal Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]=e^{-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\tilde{\jmath}(x)j(x)}\delta\delta^{\prime}\langle{\bf Q}^{\prime},{\bf R}^{\prime}|{\bf Q},{\bf R}\rangle\,, $$

where, after taking the variations, one sets ${\bf Q}={\bf Q}^{\prime}=Q$ , ${\bf R}=R+\tilde{\jmath}\mathds{1}$ and ${\bf R}^{\prime}=R+\overline{j}\mathds{1}$ . We then use (2.12) with $V_{\pm\infty}^{\prime}=V_{\pm\infty}$ and replace the boundary vectors with the left and right eigenvectors of $\mathbb{T}$ , as per the projection property (2.17). The result is

$$ \begin{split}\widetilde{\cal Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]&=\int dx\,e^{i(k-k^{\prime})x}\left(l\middle|{\cal P}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dy\,\left(\mathbb{T}+j(y)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(y)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\right)}W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\right]\middle|r\right)\\
&{}+\int dx\,dz\,e^{ikz-ik^{\prime}x}\left(l\middle|{\cal P}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dy\,\left(\mathbb{T}+j(y)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(y)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\right)}U(z)\widetilde{U}(x)\right]\middle|r\right)\,,\end{split} $$

where, in the first line, the $W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}$ insertion is assigned the position label $x$ in the path ordering, and

$$ \begin{split}U(x)&\equiv V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R}+j(x)W\otimes\mathds{1}\,,\\
\widetilde{U}(x)&\equiv\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{V}^{\prime}+R\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\,.\end{split} $$

Using the definitions (2.33) and (2.38) we can write the first line of (3.24) as

$$ \widetilde{\cal Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]\bigg|_{\text{1st line}}=\int dx\,e^{i(k-k^{\prime})x}\left(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\middle|W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\middle|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)\,. $$

This expression can be easily computed once we have solved for the vectors $|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x))$ and $(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)|$ using the differential equations (2.35) and (2.40), respectively. We write the second line of (3.24) by splitting the path ordered expression into two halves at the location $x$ :

$$ \widetilde{\cal Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]\bigg|_{\text{2nd line}}=\int dx\,e^{i(k-k^{\prime})x}\left[\left(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\middle|\widetilde{U}(x)\middle|\widehat{r}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)+\left(\widehat{l}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\middle|\widetilde{U}(x)\middle|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)\right] $$

where

$$ \begin{split}\left|\widehat{r}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)&\equiv e^{-ikx}\int_{-\infty}^{x}dz\,e^{ikz}\left.{\cal P}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{x}dy\,\left(\mathbb{T}+j(y)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(y)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\right)}U(z)\right]\middle|r\right)\,,\\
\left(\widehat{l}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right|&\equiv e^{-ikx}\int_{x}^{\infty}dz\,e^{ikz}\left(l\middle|{\cal P}\left[e^{\int_{x}^{\infty}dy\,\left(\mathbb{T}+j(y)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(y)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\right)}U(z)\right]\right.\,.\end{split} $$

The two terms in (3.27) correspond to the cases $z<x$ and $z>x$ , respectively.

Just like $|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x))$ and $(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)|$ , the vectors $\left|\widehat{r}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)$ and $\left(\widehat{l}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right|$ can be found by solving systems of ODEs that can be derived by taking $x$ -derivatives of (3.28):

$$ \begin{split}\frac{d\left|\widehat{r}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)}{dx}&=U(x)\left|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)+\left(-ik+\mathbb{T}+j(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\right)\left|\widehat{r}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)\,,\\
\frac{d\left(\widehat{l}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right|}{dx}&=-\left(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right|U(x)-\left(\widehat{l}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right|\left(ik+\mathbb{T}+j(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\right)\,.\end{split} $$

The boundary conditions are as follows. For $\left|\widehat{r}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)$ , we start solving at $x=-\infty$ . If $j$ and $\tilde{\jmath}$ have compact support, then for very negative $x$ , we have from the definition (3.28) that

$$ \left|\widehat{r}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)\approx\int_{-\infty}^{x}dz\,\left.e^{(x-z)(\mathbb{T}-ik)}(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R})\middle|r\right) $$

We are free to add $-\lambda|r)(l|(x-z)$ in the exponent for any $\lambda>0$ , provided that we work in tangent left-gauge. We can then do the $z$ integral and take $x\to-\infty$ to infer

$$ \left|\widehat{r}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(-\infty)\right)=-\frac{1}{\mathbb{T}-ik-\lambda|r)(l|}\left.(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R})\middle|r\right)\,. $$

A similar calculation gives the boundary condition for $\left(\widehat{l}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right|$ at $x=+\infty$ :

$$ \left(\widehat{l}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(\infty)\right|=-\left(l\middle|(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R})\right.\frac{1}{\mathbb{T}+ik-\lambda|r)(l|}=0\,, $$

where this expression vanishes in tangent left-gauge.

Lastly, let us discuss the generating functional for connected correlators of $a(x),a^{\dagger}(x)$ :

$$ \widetilde{\cal Z}_{\text{conn}}[\tilde{\jmath},j]\equiv\left\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k\middle|N_{\mu}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\left(\tilde{\jmath}(x)a^{\dagger}(x)+j(x)a(x)\right)}\right]\middle|V,W;k\right\rangle_{\text{conn}}\,, $$

where for simplicity we set $k^{\prime}=k$ . Due to cluster decomposition, we have

$$ \widetilde{\cal Z}_{\text{conn}}[\tilde{\jmath},j]=\lim_{k^{\prime}\to k}\left(\widetilde{\cal Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]-\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime},k^{\prime}|V,W;k\rangle{\cal Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]\right)\,, $$

where ${\cal Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]$ is the generating functional (2.27) in the underlying RCMPS, and the inner product of RQP states was given in (3.9) in tangent left-gauge. These equations imply that

$$ \begin{split}\widetilde{\cal Z}_{\text{conn}}[\tilde{\jmath},j]&=\int dx\,\biggl[\left(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\middle|W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\middle|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)-\left(l\middle|\,W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\,\middle|r\right)(l|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(\infty))\\
&{}+\left(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\middle|\widetilde{U}(x)\middle|\widehat{r}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)+\left(\widehat{l}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\middle|\widetilde{U}(x)\middle|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)\biggr]\,.\end{split} $$

This is the expression we will use in the following subsection, with $|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x))$ and $(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)|$ computed by solving (2.35) and (2.40), respectively, and $\left|\widehat{r}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)$ and $\left(\widehat{l}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right|$ determined by solving (3.29).

Note that the integrals corresponding to the terms on the first line of (3.35) are not absolutely convergent, but their sum is. Indeed, as we will show shortly, one can argue that if $j$ and $\tilde{\jmath}$ are compactly supported in the interval $[-x_{*},x_{*}]$ , then for any $|x|>x_{*}$ we have

$$ \left(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\middle|W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\middle|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)=\left(l\middle|\,W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\,\middle|r\right)(l|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(\infty))+\mathcal{O}(e^{\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits(\lambda_{2})|x|})\,,\qquad\text{for $|x|>x_{*}$}\,, $$

where $\lambda_{2}$ is the eigenvalue of $\mathbb{T}$ with the second largest real part. That the integrals on the first line of (3.35) are not absolutely convergent then follows, since the second term is manifestly $x$ -independent at large $x$ ; moreover, because of the equality (3.36), the sum of these two terms decays exponentially and hence yields an absolutely convergent integral. To show (3.36), note that for $|x|>x_{*}$ the differential equations (2.35) and (2.40) simplify to

$$ \frac{d\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)}{dx}=\mathbb{T}\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)\,,\qquad\frac{d\bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr|}{dx}=-\bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr|\mathbb{T}\,,\qquad\text{for $|x|>x_{*}$}\,. $$

Because of the projection property (2.17), these equations imply exponential approach $\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)\rightarrow\alpha_{r}|r)$ and $\bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr|\rightarrow\alpha_{l}(l|$ for $|x|>x_{*}$ with $\alpha_{r},\alpha_{l}$ constants. Let us examine the region $x>x_{*}$ first. Since $\bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(\infty)\bigr|=(l|$ we have $\bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr|=(l|$ . Meanwhile, the proportionality $\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)=\alpha_{r}|r)+\mathcal{O}(e^{\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits(\lambda_{2})x})$ implies that $\bigl|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)=|r)\bigl(l\big|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)+\mathcal{O}(e^{\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits(\lambda_{2})x})$ , since multiplying a vector proportional to $|r)$ by the projector $|r)(l|$ should leave this vector unchanged. Thus,

$$ \left(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right|=(l|\,,\qquad\left|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)=|r)\bigl(l\big|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(\infty)\bigr)+\mathcal{O}(e^{\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits(\lambda_{2})x})\,,\qquad\text{for $x>x_{*}$}\,. $$

A similar analysis shows that

$$ \bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr|=\bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(-\infty)\big|r\bigr)(l|+\mathcal{O}(e^{-\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits(\lambda_{2})x})\,,\qquad\left|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)=|r)\qquad\text{for $x<-x_{*}$}\,. $$

The equality (3.36) then follows from (3.38)–(3.39) and the fact that $\bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\big|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\bigr)$ is $x$ -independent, and hence $\bigl(l_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(-\infty)\big|r\bigr)=\bigl(l\big|r_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(\infty)\bigr)$ .

If $j$ and $\tilde{\jmath}$ do not have compact support but instead decay sufficiently fast at infinity, then (3.35) still holds. The equality (3.36) is only approximate, but the same conclusions are true.

### 3.4 Matrix elements of the Hamiltonian density

We can evaluate the connected matrix element of the Hamiltonian density ${\cal H}(0)$ in the state $|V,W;k\rangle$ , which is the main ingredient in (3.18) for determining the effective Hamiltonian. We will use the same strategy as in Section 2.5 whereby we first evaluate the matrix elements of the operators $V_{b}(0)$ , ${\cal O}_{n}(0)$ , and ${\cal H}_{\text{free}}(0)$ defined in (2.41), from which we can then construct the matrix elements of ${\cal H}(0)$ in the theories of interest (2.42).

#### 3.4.1 Matrix elements of $V_{b}(0)$

For the operator $V_{b}(0)=N_{\mu}\left[e^{b\phi(0)}\right]$ , from (2.43), we see that

$$ \left\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k\middle|V_{b}(0)\middle|V,W;k\right\rangle_{\text{conn}}=\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{\text{conn}}[bJ,bJ]\,, $$

where the functional $\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{\text{conn}}$ was computed in (3.35). In order to compute the excitation spectrum, we need to deduce the effective interaction term $\mathbf{V}_{b,k}(W)$ defined in (3.19). This is straightforward to achieve by starting from (3.40) and using the vectorization properties to write the effective operator in matrix form

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{V}_{b,k}(W) \displaystyle=l^{-1}\int dx\,\biggl[l^{\dagger}_{bJ,bJ}(x)\,W\,r_{bJ,bJ}(x)-\langle V_{b}\rangle_{Q,R}\,lWr+ \displaystyle[\widehat{l}_{bJ,bJ}^{\dagger}(x),R]\,r_{bJ,bJ}(x)+[l^{\dagger}_{bJ,bJ}(x),R]\,\widehat{r}_{bJ,bJ}(x)+ \displaystyle bJ(x)\Bigl(\widehat{l}^{\dagger}_{bJ,bJ}(x)r_{bJ,bJ}(x)+l^{\dagger}_{bJ,bJ}(x)\widehat{r}_{bJ,bJ}(x)\Bigr)\biggr]r^{-1}\,. $$

The effective operator for the sine-Gordon potential $\cos(\beta\phi)$ can then be computed as $\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{V}_{i\beta,k}(W)+\mathbf{V}_{-i\beta,k}(W))$ .

#### 3.4.2 Matrix elements of ${\cal O}_{n}(0)$

The matrix elements of ${\cal O}_{n}(0)=N_{\mu}\left[\phi(0)^{n}\right]$ can be obtained in a similar way to Section 2.5.2 by viewing (3.40) as a generating function. In particular,

$$ \left\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k\middle|{\cal O}_{n}(0)\middle|V,W;k\right\rangle_{\text{conn}}=\frac{\partial^{n}}{\partial b^{n}}\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{\text{conn}}[bJ,bJ]\bigg|_{b=0}\,. $$

We can write a more explicit formula using the definitions for $|r^{(n)}(x))$ and $(l^{(n)}(x)|$ in (2.48) and (2.53), respectively, as well as

$$ \begin{split}|\widehat{r}^{(n)}(x))\equiv\left.\frac{\partial^{n}|\widehat{r}_{bJ,bJ}(x))}{\partial b^{n}}\right|_{b=0}\,,\qquad(\widehat{l}^{(n)}(x)|\equiv\left.\frac{\partial^{n}(\widehat{l}_{bJ,bJ}(x)|}{\partial b^{n}}\right|_{b=0}\,.\end{split} $$

From (3.35), the matrix element (3.42) becomes

$$ \begin{split}&\left\langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k\middle|{\cal O}_{n}(0)\middle|V,W;k\right\rangle_{\text{conn}}\\
&\quad=\int dx\,\Biggl[-\left(l\middle|\,W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\,\middle|r\right)(l|r^{(n)}(\infty))+\sum_{p=0}^{n}\begin{pmatrix}n\\
p\end{pmatrix}\biggl[\left(l^{(p)}(x)\middle|W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\middle|r^{(n-p)}(x)\right)\\
&\quad{}+\left(l^{(p)}(x)\middle|\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{V}^{\prime}+R\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\middle|\widehat{r}^{(n-p)}(x)\right)+\left(\widehat{l}^{(p)}(x)\middle|\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{V}^{\prime}+R\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\middle|r^{(n-p)}(x)\right)\biggr]\\
&\quad{}+nJ(x)\sum_{p=0}^{n-1}\begin{pmatrix}n-1\\
p\end{pmatrix}\biggl[\left(l^{(p)}(x)\middle|\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\middle|\widehat{r}^{(n-1-p)}(x)\right)+\left(\widehat{l}^{(p)}(x)\middle|\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\middle|r^{(n-1-p)}(x)\right)\biggr]\Biggr]\,.\end{split} $$

The equations obeyed by the functions (3.43) are

$$ \begin{split}\frac{d\left|\widehat{r}^{(n)}(x)\right)}{dx}&=\left(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R}\right)\left|r^{(n)}(x)\right)+nJ(x)W\otimes\mathds{1}\left|r^{(n-1)}(x)\right)\\
&{}+\left(-ik+\mathbb{T}\right)\left|\widehat{r}^{(n)}(x)\right)+nJ(x)\left(R\otimes\mathds{1}+\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\right)\left|\widehat{r}^{(n-1)}(x)\right)\,,\\
\frac{d\left(\widehat{l}^{(n)}(x)\right|}{dx}&=-\left(l^{(n)}(x)\right|\left(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R}\right)-nJ(x)\left(l^{(n-1)}(x)\right|W\otimes\mathds{1}\\
&{}-\left(\widehat{l}^{(n)}(x)\right|\left(ik+\mathbb{T}\right)-nJ(x)\left(\widehat{l}^{(n-1)}(x)\right|\left(R\otimes\mathds{1}+\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\right)\,.\end{split} $$

with boundary conditions obtained from (3.31)–(3.32):

$$ \left|\widehat{r}^{(n)}(-\infty)\right)=\begin{cases}-\frac{1}{\mathbb{T}-ik-\lambda|r)(l|}\left.(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R})\middle|r\right)&n=0\,,\\
0&n>0\,,\end{cases}\qquad\left(\widehat{l}^{(n)}(\infty)\right|=0\,. $$

Finally, the effective term of (3.42) becomes

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{O}_{n,k}(W) \displaystyle=(l^{\dagger})^{-1}\int dx\,\,\Bigg[-\langle\mathcal{O}_{n}\rangle_{Q,R}\,l^{\dagger}Wr+\sum_{p=0}^{n}\binom{n}{p}\bigg[l^{\dagger(p)}(x)Wr^{(n-p)}(x)-R\,l^{\dagger(p)}(x)\widehat{r}^{(n-p)}(x) \displaystyle+l^{\dagger(p)}(x)R\widehat{r}^{(n-p)}(x)-R\,\widehat{l}^{\dagger(p)}(x)r^{(n-p)}(x)+\widehat{l}^{\dagger(p)}(x)Rr^{(n-p)}(x)\bigg] \displaystyle+nJ(x)\sum_{p=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{p}\Big(l^{\dagger(p)}(x)\widehat{r}^{(n-1-p)}(x)+\widehat{l}^{\dagger(p)}(x)r^{(n-1-p)}(x)\Big)\Bigg]\,r^{-1}\,, $$

where we denoted $\langle\mathcal{O}_{n}\rangle_{Q,R}\equiv\langle Q,R|\mathcal{O}_{n}(0)|Q,R\rangle$ and again used (2.21).

#### 3.4.3 Matrix elements of ${\cal H}_{\text{free}}(0)$

We now consider the matrix elements of the free part of the Hamiltonian ${\cal H}_{\text{free}}(0)$ defined in (2.41). The statement in Section 2.5.3 that the expectation value of ${\cal H}_{\text{free}}(0)$ can be computed using (2.55) generalizes to any matrix elements between momentum eigenstates of the same momenta (see Appendix A.2). This identity allows us to retrace the steps of Section 2.5.3 and write the effective free Hamiltonian as

$$ \langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k|\mathcal{H}_{\text{free}}(0)|V,W;k\rangle_{\text{conn}}=2\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\alpha\,\partial\beta}\mathcal{\widetilde{Z}_{\text{conn}}}[\alpha H,\beta H]\Bigg|_{\alpha=\beta=0}\,, $$

where $\mathcal{\widetilde{Z}}_{\text{conn}}$ is the connected generating functional defined in (3.35). To evaluate (3.35), we need to solve the ODEs (3.29). However, we encounter the same issue as for the RCMPS ansatz in Section 2.5.3; namely, that $\partial_{x}J(x)$ has a non-integrable singularity. To resolve this, we define

$$ \bigl|\widehat{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr)=e^{-F(x)}\bigl|u^{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr)\,,\qquad\bigl(\widehat{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr|=\bigl(u^{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr|e^{F(x)}\,, $$

where $e^{-F(x)}$ is the same integrating factor used in (2.64) and (2.58). It is straightforward then to show that the ODEs obeyed by $\bigl|u^{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr)$ and $\bigl(u^{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr|$ are

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d\bigl|u^{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr)}{dx} \displaystyle=e^{F(x)}U(x)e^{-F(x)}\bigl|\widetilde{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr) \displaystyle+e^{F(x)}\bigl(-ik+\mathbb{T}+\beta\mu J(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\alpha\mu J(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\bigr)e^{-F(x)}\bigl|u^{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr)\,, $$

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d\bigl(u^{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr|}{dx} \displaystyle=-\bigl(\widetilde{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr|e^{F(x)}U(x)e^{-F(x)} \displaystyle-\bigl(u^{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr|e^{F(x)}\bigl(ik+\mathbb{T}+\beta\mu J(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\alpha\mu J(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\bigr)e^{-F(x)}\,, $$

with the boundary conditions

$$ \displaystyle\left|u^{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(-\infty)\right)\equiv\left|u^{r}(-\infty)\right)=-\frac{1}{\mathbb{T}-ik-\lambda|r)(l|}\left.(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R})\middle|r\right)\,, \displaystyle\left(u^{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(\infty)\right|=0\,, $$

where $\bigl|\widetilde{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr)$ and $\bigl(\widetilde{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr|$ are defined in (2.58) and (2.64), respectively. According to (3.48), we must take derivatives of $\mathcal{\widetilde{Z}}[\alpha H,\beta H]_{\text{conn}}$ with respect to $\alpha$ and $\beta$ , which requires that we solve two ODE systems: one for $\bigl|u^{r\,(n,m)}(x)\bigr)$ and one for $\bigl(u^{l\,(n,m)}(x)\bigr|$ , where we again use the notation $f^{(n,m)}\equiv\left.\frac{\partial^{n+m}f}{\partial\alpha^{n}\partial\beta^{m}}\right|_{\alpha=\beta=0}$ . Having solved for $\bigl|u^{r\,(n,m)}(x)\bigr),\bigl(u^{l\,(n,m)}(x)\bigr|$ , we can deduce the derivatives of $\bigl|\widehat{r}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr)$ and $\bigl(\widehat{l}_{\alpha H,\beta H}(x)\bigr|$ using (3.49). We refer the reader to Appendix B for detailed equations.

This determines all quantities needed to evaluate (3.48) and we can combine them into an expression for the effective free Hamiltonian

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{H}_{k} \displaystyle(W)=2{l}^{-1}\int dx\,\Bigg[-\frac{1}{2}\langle\mathcal{H}_{\text{free}}\rangle_{Q,R}\,lWr+\,[\widehat{l}^{\dagger\,(1,1)}(x),R]\,r+[\widehat{l}^{\dagger\,(0,1)}(x),R]\,r^{(1,0)}(x) \displaystyle+[\widehat{l}^{\dagger\,(1,0)}(x),R]\,r^{(0,1)}(x)+[\widehat{l}^{\dagger},R]\,r^{(1,1)}(x) \displaystyle+\,[l^{\dagger\,(1,1)}(x),R]\,\widehat{r}+[l^{\dagger\,(0,1)}(x),R]\,\widehat{r}^{(1,0)}(x)+[l^{\dagger\,(1,0)}(x),R]\,\widehat{r}^{(0,1)}(x)+[l^{\dagger},R]\,\widehat{r}^{(1,1)}(x) \displaystyle+\,l^{\dagger\,(1,1)}(x)\,W\,r+l^{\dagger\,(0,1)}(x)\,W\,r^{(1,0)}(x)+l^{\dagger\,(1,0)}(x)\,W\,r^{(0,1)}(x)+l^{\dagger}\,W\,r^{(1,1)}(x) \displaystyle+\,J(x)\Big(\widehat{l}^{\dagger\,(1,0)}(x)\,r+l^{\dagger\,(1,0)}(x)\,\widehat{r}\Big)\Bigg]\,r^{-1}\,, $$

where we defined $\langle\mathcal{H}_{\text{free}}\rangle_{Q,R}\equiv\langle Q,R|\mathcal{H}_{\text{free}}(0)|Q,R\rangle$ .

### 3.5 Dispersion relation at large momentum

In Section 2.5, we saw that the RCMPS ansatz encodes the correct relativistic short distance behavior of correlation functions. Analogously, we will now show that the RQP ansatz at large momentum recovers the Lorentz-covariant dispersion $\omega(k)\sim|k|$ . To that end, we need to determine the large momentum limit of the connected matrix elements of the various ingredients (3.19) used for computing the effective Hamiltonian.

The connected Hamiltonian matrix elements can be computed in terms of the generating functional (3.35), which we find convenient to rewrite as

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{\cal Z}_{\text{conn}}[\tilde{\jmath},j] \displaystyle=\int dx\,\left(l\middle|{\cal P}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dz\,\left(\mathbb{T}+j(z)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(z)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\right)}\left\{W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}-(l|(W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime})|r)\right\}\right]\middle|r\right) \displaystyle}{\displaystyle+\int dx\,dy\,e^{ik(x-y)}\left(l\middle|{\cal P}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dz\,\left(\mathbb{T}+j(z)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{j}(z)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}\right)}U(x)\widetilde{U}(y)\right]\middle|r\right)\,, $$

where, in the first line, the insertion in the path ordering is at $x$ , and in the second line the quantities $U,\widetilde{U}$ were defined in (3.25). The first line is independent of $k$ , while the second line takes the form of Fourier transforms with respect to $x,y$ . For integrable sources such as $j,\tilde{\jmath}\propto J$ , which are relevant for the interaction potentials, the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma ensures that the Fourier transforms decay. Thus, the interaction potential does not give rise to an asymptotically increasing energy at large momentum. For the free part of the Hamiltonian, the necessary source function is proportional to $H(x)=(\mu-\partial_{x})J(x)$ which is not integrable due to $\partial_{x}J(x)$ and one has to take care in the application of the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma. The connected matrix element of the free Hamiltonian (3.48) can be written as

$$ \langle V^{\prime},W^{\prime};k|\mathcal{H}_{\text{free}}(0)|V,W;k\rangle_{\text{conn}}=2\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\alpha\,\partial\beta}\mathcal{\widetilde{Z}_{\text{conn}}}[\alpha H,\beta H]\Bigg|_{\alpha=\beta=0}=I_{1}+I_{2}+I_{3}+I_{4}+I_{5}\,, $$

where the integrals $I_{i}$ are defined as

$$ \begin{split}I_{1}&=2\int dx\,dy\,e^{ik(x-y)}\,H(x)H(y)\left(l\middle|{\cal P}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dz\,\mathbb{T}}(W\otimes\mathds{1})_{x}\,(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime})_{y}\right]\middle|r\right)\,,\\
I_{2}&=2\int dx\,dy\,dz\,e^{ik(x-y)}\,H(x)H(z)\left(l\middle|{\cal P}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dz^{\prime}\,\mathbb{T}}(W\otimes\mathds{1})_{x}\,(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R})_{z}\,\widetilde{U}_{0}(y)\right]\middle|r\right)\,,\\
I_{3}&=2\int dx\,dy\,dz\,e^{ik(x-y)}\,H(z)H(y)\left(l\middle|{\cal P}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dz^{\prime}\,\mathbb{T}}(R\otimes\mathds{1})_{z}\,U_{0}(x)\,(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime})_{y}\right]\middle|r\right)\,,\\
I_{4}&=2\int dx\,dy\,dz\,dz^{\prime}\,e^{ik(x-y)}\,H(z)H(z^{\prime})\\
&{}\qquad\quad\times\left(l\middle|{\cal P}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dz^{\prime\prime}\,\mathbb{T}}(R\otimes\mathds{1})_{z}\,(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R})_{z^{\prime}}\,U_{0}(x)\,\widetilde{U}_{0}(y)\right]\middle|r\right)\,,\\
I_{5}&=2\int dx\,dz\,dz^{\prime}\,H(z)H(z^{\prime})\\
&{}\qquad\quad\times\left(l\middle|{\cal P}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dz^{\prime\prime}\,\mathbb{T}}(R\otimes\mathds{1})_{z}\,(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R})_{z^{\prime}}\,\bigl\{W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}-(l|(W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime})|r)\bigr\}_{x}\right]\middle|r\right)\,,\end{split} $$

where we denoted $U$ and $\tilde{U}$ evaluated at $\alpha=\beta=0$ as $U_{0}$ and $\tilde{U}_{0}$ , respectively, and indicated the insertion points in the path-ordering by subscripts, such as in $(W\otimes 1)_{x}$ . We begin by examining the large momentum behavior of $I_{1}$ . Since the path-ordered exponentials preserve the fixed points $(l|,|r)$ , we can simplify the integral and insert $H(x)=(\mu-\partial_{x})J(x)$

$$ \begin{split}I_{1}&=2\int dx\,dy\,e^{ik(x-y)}\,\Bigl(\mu^{2}J(x)J(y)-\mu J(y)\partial_{x}J(x)-\mu J(x)\partial_{y}J(y)+\partial_{x}J(x)\partial_{y}J(y)\Bigr)\\
&\times\left(l\middle|\theta(x-y)(W\otimes\mathds{1})\,e^{\mathbb{T}(x-y)}\,(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime})+\theta(y-x)(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime})\,e^{\mathbb{T}(y-x)}\,(W\otimes\mathds{1})\middle|r\right)\,.\end{split} $$

The term containing $J(x)J(y)$ is integrable and decays at large momentum due to the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma. The terms containing $J(y)\partial_{x}J(x)$ and $J(x)\partial_{y}J(y)$ cancel exactly. To see this we use the identity

$$ \int dx\,dy\,f(y)\partial_{x}g(x)S(x-y)=-\int dx\,dy\,g(x)\partial_{y}f(y)S(x-y)\,, $$

which holds for functions that decay at infinity and is easily proven by integration by parts. The remaining term in (3.57) contains $\partial_{x}J(x)\partial_{y}J(y)$ and thus the large momentum behavior of $I_{1}$ is

$$ \displaystyle I_{1} \displaystyle=2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\int^{x}_{-\infty}dy\,e^{ik(x-y)}\partial_{x}J(x)\partial_{y}J(y)\,\bigl(l\bigr|(W\otimes\mathds{1})\,e^{\mathbb{T}(x-y)}(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime})\bigl|r\bigr) \displaystyle}{\displaystyle+2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dy\int^{y}_{-\infty}dx\,e^{ik(x-y)}\partial_{x}J(x)\partial_{y}J(y)\,\bigl(l\bigr|(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime})e^{\mathbb{T}(y-x)}(W\otimes\mathds{1})\bigl|r\bigr)+o(|k|^{0})\,, $$

Upon integration by parts, we find
