$$ \displaystyle I_{1} \displaystyle=2k^{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\int^{x}_{-\infty}dy\,e^{ik(x-y)}J(x)J(y)\,\bigl(l\bigr|(W\otimes\mathds{1})\,e^{\mathbb{T}(x-y)}(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime})\bigl|r\bigr) \displaystyle}{\displaystyle+2k^{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dy\int^{y}_{-\infty}dx\,e^{ik(x-y)}J(x)J(y)\,\bigl(l\bigr|(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime})e^{\mathbb{T}(y-x)}(W\otimes\mathds{1})\bigl|r\bigr) \displaystyle}{\displaystyle-4ik\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\int^{x}_{-\infty}dy\,e^{ik(x-y)}J(x)J(y)\,\bigl(l\bigr|(W\otimes\mathds{1})\,\mathbb{T}\,e^{\mathbb{T}(x-y)}(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime})\bigl|r\bigr) \displaystyle}{\displaystyle+4ik\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dy\int^{y}_{-\infty}dx\,e^{ik(x-y)}J(x)J(y)\,\bigl(l\bigr|(\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime})\,\mathbb{T}\,e^{\mathbb{T}(y-x)}(W\otimes\mathds{1})\bigl|r\bigr)+\mathcal{O}(|k|^{0})\,, $$

where the remainder contains terms that decay according to the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma and a divergent term independent of $k$ . However, this divergence must be canceled in (3.55), because the effective Hamiltonian is finite, as shown in (3.53). The remaining integrals in (3.60) can be computed using the spectral decomposition $e^{\mathbb{T}(x-y)}=\sum_{n}e^{\lambda_{n}(x-y)}|r_{n})(l_{n}|$ , which reduces the integrals in (3.60) to the scalar integral

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\int^{x}_{-\infty}dy\,e^{ik(x-y)}J(x)J(y)e^{\lambda(x-y)}=\frac{i}{4\pi k}\log\frac{4k^{2}}{\mu^{2}}+\frac{1}{4|k|}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{k^{2}}\log\frac{k^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)\,. $$

Adding up the terms in (3.60), and noting that the last two lines contribute only at $\mathcal{O}\bigl(\log\frac{k^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\bigr)$ , we get

$$ \displaystyle I_{1} \displaystyle\approx\left(\frac{ik}{2\pi}\log\frac{4k^{2}}{\mu^{2}}+\frac{|k|}{2}\right)\sum_{n}\bigl(l\bigr|W\otimes\mathds{1}\bigl|r_{n}\bigr)\bigl(l_{n}\bigr|\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\bigl|r\bigr) \displaystyle}{\displaystyle+\left(-\frac{ik}{2\pi}\log\frac{4k^{2}}{\mu^{2}}+\frac{|k|}{2}\right)\sum_{n}\bigl(l\bigr|\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\bigl|r_{n}\bigr)\bigl(l_{n}\bigr|W\otimes\mathds{1}\bigl|r\bigr)+\mathcal{O}\left(\log\frac{k^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)\,. $$

In this expression we recognize the sum over $n$ as the resolution of identity, and therefore

$$ \displaystyle I_{1} \displaystyle\approx|k|\bigl(l\bigr|W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\bigl|r\bigr)+\mathcal{O}\left(\log\frac{k^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)\,. $$

A similar analysis for the remaining integrals in (3.55) shows that $I_{2}=\mathcal{O}\left(\log\frac{k^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)$ , $I_{3}=\mathcal{O}\left(\log\frac{k^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)$ , $I_{4}=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\mu}{|k|}\log\frac{k^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)$ , and $I_{5}$ is $k$ -independent. Consequently, the large $k$ behavior of the dispersion relation follows directly from (3.17)

$$ \omega(k)\approx|k|+\mathcal{O}\left(\log\frac{k^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)\,,\quad|k|\rightarrow\infty\,. $$

This shows that the large momentum leading contribution to the effective Hamiltonian of the RQP is $|k|$ regardless of the specifics of the state $|V,W;k\rangle$ . Thus, the RQP ansatz naturally encodes the expected relativistic behavior. In particular, the derivation of the UV behavior of the dispersion $\omega(k)$ relied crucially on the use of $a^{\dagger}(x)$ in the construction of the ansatz (3.1), as it gave rise to the kernel $J(x)$ and in turn the $\frac{1}{|k|}$ behavior in (3.61). On the other hand, since the ansatz (3.1) is not Lorentz covariant, the convergence of $\omega(k)$ to the expected relativistic expression $\sqrt{M^{2}+k^{2}}$ at small momenta will serve as an important consistency check of our method.

### 3.6 Solitonic excitations

The RQP ansatz for the particle-like excitations (3.1) can be generalized to solitonic excitations [23] interpolating between two degenerate vacua described by $|Q_{1},R_{1}\rangle$ at $x\rightarrow\infty$ and $|Q_{2},R_{2}\rangle$ at $x\rightarrow-\infty$ . In particular, solitonic excitations are implemented by substituting $(Q,R)\rightarrow(Q_{1},R_{1})$ to the left of the local perturbation in (3.1) and $(Q,R)\rightarrow(Q_{2},R_{2})$ to the right of it, yielding

$$ \displaystyle|V,W;k\rangle_{\text{sol}} \displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,e^{ikx}V_{+\infty}^{\dagger}\mathcal{P}e^{\int_{x}^{\infty}dy\,Q_{1}\otimes\mathds{1}+R_{1}\otimes a^{\dagger}(y)}\left(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes a^{\dagger}(x)\right) \displaystyle}{\displaystyle\times\mathcal{P}e^{\int_{-\infty}^{x}dy\,Q_{2}\otimes\mathds{1}+R_{2}\otimes a^{\dagger}(y)}V_{-\infty}|0\rangle\,. $$

For the solitonic excitations, the momentum $k$ in (3.65) is ambiguous as one can rephase, say, the vacuum parametrized by $(Q_{2},R_{2})$ by $Q_{2}\rightarrow Q_{2}+i\alpha\mathds{1}$ for $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ , which is equivalent to $k\rightarrow k+\alpha$ and an overall phase. This ambiguity does not appear for the particle-like excitations (3.1) because rephasing both sides simultaneously contributes an overall phase to the state.

The solitonic RQP ansatz is also invariant under a gauge transformation analogous to (3.7)

$$ V\rightarrow V+XQ_{2}-Q_{1}X+ikX\,,\qquad W\rightarrow W+XR_{2}-R_{1}X\,. $$

Similarly, one can go to the tangent left-gauge where $V$ can be eliminated as $V=-l_{1}^{-1}R_{1}^{\dagger}l_{1}W$ , where one uses $R_{1}$ as the gauge choice referring to the left vacuum $|Q_{1},R_{1}\rangle$ . The derivation of the effective Hamiltonian in Section 3.4 still applies with only minor changes to keep track of the two vacua. These modifications are necessary because $|V,W;k\rangle_{\text{sol}}$ does not look like a tangent vector (cf. (3.2)) above either of the two vacuum states.

To derive the effective Hamiltonian for the solitonic RQP ansatz (3.65), it will be convenient to embed the two RCMPSs in a doubled RCMPS ansatz $|\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{R}\rangle$ with

$$ \mathcal{Q}\equiv\begin{pmatrix}Q_{1}&0\\
0&Q_{2}\end{pmatrix}\,,\qquad\mathcal{R}\equiv\begin{pmatrix}R_{1}&0\\
0&R_{2}\end{pmatrix}\,, $$

where $\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{R}$ are now $2\chi\times 2\chi$ matrices and the corresponding boundary vectors for the RCMPS are similarly constructed as direct sums. The solitonic ansatz (3.65) can then be considered a particle-like RQP over the doubled vacuum $|\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{R}\rangle$ . In particular, the choice of tangent vector

$$ \mathcal{V}\equiv\begin{pmatrix}0&V\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}\,,\quad\mathcal{W}\equiv\begin{pmatrix}0&W\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}\,, $$

immediately leads to the identification

$$ |\mathcal{V},\mathcal{W};k\rangle=|V,W;k\rangle_{\text{sol}}\,. $$

The LHS of (3.69) can be treated as a non-topological RQP as in Section 3.3 allowing us to reuse the framework derived for particle-like excitations. In particular, one has to evaluate the generating functional (3.35) using (3.67) and (3.68) and simplify the formulas using the block structure of the matrices. An important caveat is subtraction of the connected part of the matrix element in (3.15). As the two vacuum states are degenerate, they agree on the subtraction as it only depends on the vacuum energy density. However, we would like to compute the effective Hamiltonian for each term in the Hamiltonian separately, but this is not a well-defined operation if the two vacua do not agree on the expectation value of each term separately. Computing the effective Hamiltonian term by term will in general give rise to divergences that cancel only once added up to the full effective Hamiltonian. Below, we will use a symmetric subtraction of the connected part which will render each term of effective Hamiltonian finite but physically meaningless when the VEVs do not agree between the left and right vacua. This ambiguity cancels in the sum of the separate terms.

Upon carrying out the above program, equations are again expressed in terms of $\chi\times\chi$ matrices and the solitonic generalization of the generating functional for the connected matrix elements $\widetilde{\cal Z}_{\text{conn}}[\tilde{\jmath},j]$ is

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{\cal Z}^{\text{sol}}_{\text{conn}}[\tilde{\jmath},j] \displaystyle=\int dx\,\biggl[\left({l_{1}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\middle|W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\middle|{r_{2}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)-\left(l_{1}\middle|\,W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\,\middle|r_{2}\right)[(l_{1}|{r_{1}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(\infty))+(l_{2}|{r_{2}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(\infty))]/2 \displaystyle{}+\left({l_{1}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\middle|\tilde{U}_{1}(x)\middle|{\widehat{r}}^{\text{sol}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)+\left({\widehat{l}}^{\text{sol}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\middle|\tilde{U}_{2}(x)\middle|{r_{2}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)\biggr]\,, $$

where $\big(l_{a,\tilde{\jmath},j}|$ and $\big|r_{a,\tilde{\jmath},j}\big)$ refer to (2.38) and (2.33), respectively, as computed in the state $|Q_{a},R_{a}\rangle$ for $a=1,2$ . Further, we defined the matrices

$$ \begin{split}U_{a}(x)&\equiv V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R}_{a}+j(x)W\otimes\mathds{1}\,,\\
\widetilde{U}_{a}(x)&\equiv\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{V}^{\prime}+R_{a}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\,.\end{split} $$

and the generalization of $\left(\widehat{l}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right|,\left|\widehat{r}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)$ defined by the ODEs

$$ \begin{split}\frac{d\left|\widehat{r}^{\text{sol}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)}{dx}&=U_{2}(x)\left|{r_{2}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)+\left(-ik+\mathbb{T}_{1,2}+j(x)R_{1}\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}_{2}\right)\left|\widehat{r}^{\text{sol}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)\,,\\
\frac{d\left(\widehat{l}^{\text{sol}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right|}{dx}&=-\left({l_{1}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right|U_{1}(x)-\left(\widehat{l}^{\text{sol}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right|\left(ik+\mathbb{T}_{2,1}+j(x)R_{2}\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}_{1}\right)\,.\end{split} $$

and the boundary condition1212 12 The regulator $-\lambda|r)(l|(x-z)$ we used in (3.31) is now not needed, since the mixed transfer matrix has no zero eigenvalues, rendering $(\mathbb{T}_{1,2}-ik)$ invertible for generic $k$ .

$$ \displaystyle\left|\widehat{r}^{\text{sol}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(-\infty)\right) \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\mathbb{T}_{1,2}-ik}\left.(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R}_{2})\middle|r_{2}\right)\,, \displaystyle\left(\widehat{l}^{\text{sol}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(\infty)\right| \displaystyle=-\left(l_{1}\middle|(V\otimes\mathds{1}+W\otimes\overline{R}_{1})\right.\frac{1}{\mathbb{T}_{2,1}+ik}=0\,, $$

with the notation for the mixed transfer matrix

$$ \mathbb{T}_{a,b}=Q_{a}\otimes\mathds{1}+\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{Q}_{b}+R_{a}\otimes\overline{R}_{b}\,. $$

To see that the symmetric subtraction of the connected part in the first line of (3.70) makes the integral finite notice that if one repeats the derivation of (3.36) for $\left({l_{1}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\middle|W\otimes\overline{W}^{\prime}\middle|{r_{2}}_{\tilde{\jmath},j}(x)\right)$ then one finds that it is proportional to the VEV of $|Q_{1},R_{1}\rangle$ for large positive $x$ and to the VEV of $|Q_{2},R_{2}\rangle$ for large negative $x$ . Thus, subtracting the average of the VEVs in (3.70) correctly cancels the divergence when the integral is done symmetrically about $x=0$ .

From (3.70), one can specialize to the necessary operators (2.41) as done for the particle-like RQP in Section 3.4.

## 4 Applications

In this section, we will apply the RCMPS and RQP frameworks developed in the previous section to the sine-Gordon and $\phi^{4}$ models (2.3). To extract the excitation spectrum of a scalar field theory, we first need to solve for the RCMPS representing the vacuum and then solve for the RQP energies by finding the low-lying eigenvalues of the effective Hamiltonian. The vacuum state is determined by minimizing the expectation value of the Hamiltonian density, as computed in Section 2.5, over the space of RCMPSs. This is a non-linear optimization problem, which we solve using a gradient-descent-type solver. Once the vacuum RCMPS is known, the effective Hamiltonian can be constructed as in Section 3.4, and we can then solve for its low-lying eigenvalues. We give further details on the numerical implementation in Appendix C.

### 4.1 Sine-Gordon model

#### 4.1.1 Definition and excitation spectrum

The sine-Gordon model is a real scalar theory with a rich spectrum of particle and solitonic excitations, which furthermore is integrable [25]. Hence, the sine-Gordon model serves as a highly non-trivial benchmark of our numerical setup. The Hamiltonian density is

$$ \mathcal{H}_{\text{sG}}=N_{m}\left[\frac{1}{2}\pi^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}+\frac{m^{2}}{\beta^{2}}(1-\cos(\beta\phi))\right]\,, $$

where, relative to (2.42), we took the normal ordering mass to be $\mu=m$ . Despite the interaction potential not being polynomial, the Hamiltonian (4.1) is still UV finite for $\beta^{2}<4\pi$ [32]; further renormalization is required for $\beta^{2}\geq 4\pi$ [33]. In this work, we restrict ourselves to $\beta^{2}<4\pi$ . In this range, the spectrum of excitations consists of a soliton and an anti-soliton, also called kink and anti-kink, with equal masses given by [34]

$$ \frac{M_{\text{sol}}}{m}=\frac{2\pi^{\frac{\xi(\beta)}{2}}\Gamma\left(\frac{\xi(\beta)}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{1+\xi(\beta)}{2}\right)}\left(\frac{\mu(\beta)\Gamma\left(1-\frac{\beta^{2}}{8\pi}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{\beta^{2}}{8\pi}\right)}\right)^{\frac{4\pi}{8\pi-\beta^{2}}}\,,\qquad\text{with}\qquad\begin{aligned} \xi(\beta)&=\frac{\beta^{2}}{8\pi-\beta^{2}}\,,\\
\mu(\beta)&=\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{\gamma\beta^{2}}{4\pi}\right)}{2^{1-\frac{\beta^{2}}{4\pi}}\beta^{2}}\,,\end{aligned} $$

where $\gamma$ is the Euler-Mascheroni constant, as well as a number of stable particles known as breathers.1313 13 The quantity $\mu(\beta)$ in (4.2) should not be confused with the normal ordering mass used in previous sections. The relationship between the masses of the breathers and the mass of the soliton was first determined by a semi-classical analysis in [35] and later confirmed to be exact using integrability [25]:

$$ M_{n}=2\sin\left(\frac{\pi n\xi(\beta)}{2}\right)M_{\text{sol}}\,,\qquad n=1,2,\ldots,n_{\text{max}}\,, $$

with $n_{\text{max}}$ the largest integer such that $n_{\text{max}}<\frac{1}{\xi(\beta)}$ . Roughly speaking, the solitons can be interpreted as interpolating between two adjacent equivalent classical minima $\phi_{\text{min}}\in\frac{2\pi\mathbb{Z}}{\beta}$ of the interaction potential, and the breathers can be thought of as soliton-anti-soliton bound states.1414 14 Normal-ordering respects the shift symmetry $\phi\rightarrow\phi+\frac{2\pi\mathbb{Z}}{\beta}$ of the bare Hamiltonian. In the weak coupling limit $\beta^{2}\ll 1$ , the particle spectrum contains arbitrarily many stable particle states with masses $M_{n}=nm+\mathcal{O}(\beta^{2})$ that can be interpreted as loosely bound states of $n$ elementary quanta of the free $\beta^{2}=0$ theory. ### 4.2 $\phi^{4}$ theory

We now turn to the $\phi^{4}$ theory, which, despite its simplicity, is not integrable and exhibits an array of interesting physical phenomena. The $\phi^{4}$ theory is defined as a free massive scalar of mass $m$ deformed by a quartic self-coupling of strength $g$ , with Hamiltonian density

$$ \mathcal{H}_{\phi^{4}}=N_{m}\left[\frac{1}{2}\pi^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}m^{2}\phi^{2}+g\phi^{4}\right]\,, $$

where we again have taken the normal ordering mass to be $\mu=m$ (see (2.42)). The Hamiltonian density (4.4) has an internal $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ symmetry $\phi\rightarrow-\phi$ , which is preserved by the normal-ordering procedure. Even though we will only consider $m^{2}>0$ , the symmetry breaks spontaneously at some $g_{c}>0$ because the normal-ordering of the quartic term effectively renormalizes the mass term. The critical value of the coupling has been studied in many works, such as [36, 27], and it is approximately ${g_{c}}\approx 2.77{m^{2}}$ in the scheme defined by (4.4) (see [37] for a recent study with a comparison of the estimates in the literature). The quantum phase transition at $g=g_{c}$ is in the Ising universality class.

In the perturbative regime $g\ll m^{2}$ , the $\phi^{4}$ interaction is repulsive and the spectrum consists of only the fundamental particle created by $\phi$ . This particle remains the only stable particle in the symmetry preserving phase $0\leq g<g_{c}$ and its mass decreases from $m$ at $g=0$ to zero at the critical coupling $g=g_{c}$ .

To understand the spectrum in the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ -broken phase, for $g>g_{c}$ , it is convenient to make use of the strong/weak duality transformation known as Chang duality [38]. The transformation is derived by changing the normal-ordering scale in the Hamiltonian (4.4) to a mass scale $\widetilde{m}$ such that the classical potential exhibits spontaneous symmetry breaking. Furthermore, the mass $\widetilde{m}$ is chosen such that the excitations above these classical minima have classical mass equal to $\widetilde{m}$ . As we will see, the correct Hamiltonian density to consider is [38]

$$ \mathcal{H}_{\phi^{4}}=N_{\widetilde{m}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\pi^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}\widetilde{m}^{2}\phi^{2}+g\phi^{4}\right]\,, $$

which for a proper choice of $\widetilde{m}$ equals the original Hamiltonian density (4.4) up to an additive constant, as we will see. Note that in (4.5), the mass term is negative, giving rise to two symmetry-broken classical minima, and the precise coefficient of the $\phi^{2}$ term is chosen such that it gives the correct normalizations of the mass term for the fluctuations around these minima. Indeed, the two minima are at $\phi=\pm\frac{\widetilde{m}}{\sqrt{8g}}$ , and, if we write $\phi=\tilde{\phi}\pm\frac{\widetilde{m}}{\sqrt{8g}}$ , the Hamiltonian density (4.5) takes the form

$$ \mathcal{H}_{\phi^{4}}=N_{\widetilde{m}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\tilde{\pi}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\tilde{\phi})^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{m}^{2}\tilde{\phi}^{2}\pm\sqrt{2g}\,\widetilde{m}\tilde{\phi}^{3}+g\tilde{\phi}^{4}\right]\,, $$

where we neglected an additive constant shift in the energy. Note that the negative mass term $-\frac{1}{4}\widetilde{m}^{2}\phi^{2}$ in (4.5) results in the canonical mass term $+\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{m}^{2}\tilde{\phi}^{2}$ in (4.6).

To determine the $\widetilde{m}$ that makes (4.4) and (4.5) equal, recall the following re-normal-ordering identities

$$ \displaystyle N_{m}\left[\frac{1}{2}\pi^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}\right] \displaystyle=N_{\widetilde{m}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\pi^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}\right]+\text{const.}\,, \displaystyle N_{m}[\phi^{2}] \displaystyle=N_{\widetilde{m}}[\phi^{2}]+\text{const.}\,, \displaystyle N_{m}[\phi^{4}] \displaystyle=N_{\widetilde{m}}\left[\phi^{4}+\frac{3}{2\pi}\log\left(\frac{m^{2}}{\widetilde{m}^{2}}\right)\phi^{2}\right]+\text{const.}\,. $$

Equating the Hamiltonian densities (4.4) and (4.5) (up to a constant shift) and using (4.7) yields the relation

$$ \frac{6}{\pi}\log(Y)+\frac{1}{Y}=\frac{6}{\pi}\log(X)-\frac{2}{X}\,, $$

where we defined the effective dimensionless couplings $X\equiv\frac{g}{m^{2}}$ and $Y\equiv\frac{g}{\widetilde{m}^{2}}$ . The relation (4.8) is plotted in Figure 4. For $X>X_{*}\approx 2.26$ , (4.8) has two real solutions, $Y_{1}(X)$ and $Y_{2}(X)$ , with $Y_{1}(X)\leq Y_{2}(X)$ .1515 15 The explicit form of the two branches can be written in terms of the Lambert $W$ -function

$$ Y_{1}(X)=-\frac{\pi}{6W_{-1}\left(-\frac{\pi}{6X}\exp{\frac{\pi}{3X}}\right)}\,,\qquad Y_{2}(X)=-\frac{\pi}{6W_{0}\left(-\frac{\pi}{6X}\exp{\frac{\pi}{3X}}\right)}\,. $$

As demonstrated in Figure 4, the lower branch $Y_{1}(X)$ sends large dimensionless coupling $X$ to small $Y$ , corresponding to a strong/weak duality. At large $X$ , this solution has the leading strong-coupling behavior

$$ Y_{1}(X)\approx\frac{\pi}{6}\frac{1}{\log X}\,. $$

Furthermore, since $X_{*}<\frac{g_{c}}{m^{2}}$ , the dual formulation (4.5) can also access part of the symmetry preserving phase. The upper branch $Y_{2}(X)$ sends strong coupling to strong coupling and is not of interest for our purposes, so in the following discussion we take $Y=Y_{1}(X)$ .

#### 4.2.1 Numerical results

In Figure 5, we show our results for the spectrum of excitations in the formulation (4.4). As expected, for $g<g_{c}$ we find a single stable particle below the two-particle continuum. As the coupling is tuned to the critical value, the mass gap closes, and immediately beyond the critical point the only stable excitation is the soliton. Linearly extrapolating the $\chi=28$ data points closest to the phase transition to vanishing mass, we obtain the estimate $g_{c}/m^{2}\approx 2.78$ for the critical coupling. This value is in agreement with the literature [27]. Furthermore, at $\frac{g}{m^{2}}\approx 8.7$ , a stable particle emerges from the two-soliton continuum.

Note that the slope of the particle mass just below the transition and the slope of the soliton mass just above the transition are equal and opposite. To understand this, we start by noticing that the low-energy physics near the critical point $g_{c}$ is described by the 2d Ising model deformed by the energy operator $\epsilon$ , namely $S=S_{\text{Ising}}+\lambda\int d^{2}x\,\epsilon$ with $\lambda\sim(g-g_{c})$ . By fermionization, this effective description is equivalent to the free Majorana CFT deformed by a mass term, $S=S_{\text{Majorana}}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\int d^{2}x\,\overline{\psi}\psi$ . Thus, the mass gap on either side of the phase transition is due to the massive Majorana fermion and is proportional to $|\lambda|\sim|g-g_{c}|$ . In the bosonic description, the fermionic particle excitation is represented as a particle for $\lambda<0$ and as a soliton for $\lambda>0$ .

Near the critical coupling, our numerical results yield solitons of negative mass for small values of the bond dimension $\chi$ . This phenomenon can be understood as follows. For finite bond dimension, the symmetry properties of the RCMPS of lowest energy denisty need not coincide with those of the physical vacuum. In particular, as the critical coupling is approached from the symmetry-preserving side $g<g_{c}$ , the optimal RCMPS of bond dimension $\chi$ breaks the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ symmetry at a value of the coupling $g_{c,\chi}$ less than the physical $g_{c}$ [1]. Moreover, as the bond dimension is increased, the observed critical coupling $g_{c,\chi}$ converges to the physical value. The negative soliton mass is a signal that the optimal RCMPS is not the minimum energy state in the full Hilbert space.

## 5 Discussion

In this paper, we developed the framework for the RQP ansatz for relativistic field theories in $(1+1)$ d. This framework allows one to determine not just the spectrum of low-lying particle excitations, but also of solitons between distinct degenerate vacua. Building on the RCMPS framework, the RQP ansatz is defined directly in the continuum, at infinite volume, and without an explicit UV cutoff. We presented the necessary formalism for an efficient numerical implementation of the RQP ansatz, and we showed that the large momentum limit of the ansatz reproduces an ultra-relativistic dispersion. To demonstrate the validity of the RQP ansatz, we studied the sine-Gordon model and numerically reproduced the breather and soliton masses along with their relativistic dispersions. Finally, we studied the $\phi^{4}$ theory and determined the particle and soliton spectrum for all values of the coupling.

There are various future directions that are worth mentioning. An interesting scalar field theory that fits within the framework developed in this paper is the Landau-Ginzburg description of the tri-critical Ising model deformed by some relevant operator in terms of a sextic interaction potential. In [41], it was argued that certain deformations of the tri-critical Ising model give rise to degenerate vacua exchanged by non-invertible symmetries. Furthermore, for certain deformations, the non-invertible symmetries group the soliton (and anti-soliton) between the vacua and a particle above one of the vacua into a degenerate multiplet. Using the RQP ansatz to study a sextic scalar field theory, one could directly probe this multiplet. However, in order to preserve non-invertible symmetry, one would need to simultaneously fine-tune multiple parameters.

The RQP ansatz can naturally be adapted to other studies using RCMPS. In particular, one could study the excitation spectrum in the multi-scalar field theories of [21]. With multiple species, it is necessary to impose further regularity conditions on the RCMPS ansatz to obtain a finite energy density. These bosonic regularity conditions were studied in [21] and also extended to a characterization at the level of the tangent space. It would be interesting to understand how the tangent space restriction relates to the finiteness of the quasiparticle excitation energy. Similarly, one could also study an RQP based on RCMPSs for Dirac fermions, which effectively has two species of fermions for which one also needs regularity conditions to yield finite energy density [31].

Another avenue is to adapt methods from discrete MPS that have not previously been studied using CMPS. One such MPS construction is the two-particle scattering ansatz of [42], which allowed the authors to directly study the S-matrix for 2-to-2 scattering of the quasiparticles. The two-particle ansatz is constructed by summing over two local perturbations of the vacuum state with distinct variational parameters as a function of the distance between the insertions. To construct an RCMPS analog of this ansatz, one would, in particular, need to parameterize these variational parameters as a function of continuous distance, unlike for MPS where the lattice offers a natural discretization of the distance.

## Appendix C Numerical implementation

In this appendix, we describe further implementation details for the numerical work presented in Section 4. All numerical calculations are carried out in the left-gauge (2.26) for the RCMPS ansatz, which enables us to eliminate the redundant components of $Q$ by writing [31]

$$ Q=-iK-\frac{1}{2}R^{\dagger}R\,, $$

where $K$ is a Hermitian matrix. For the RQP ansatz, we used the tangent left-gauge (3.8).

The vacuum state is determined by minimizing the expectation value of the Hamiltonian density, as computed in Section 2.5, over the space of RCMPSs. This is a non-linear optimization problem and requires one to determine the gradient of the energy density to efficiently solve it. The expression for the gradient of a given expectation value can be derived using the same methods as used for the RQP in Section 3.3 (see [1]). As an example, we can consider the gradient $M_{b}$ of the expectation value $\langle V_{b}\rangle$ for real $b$ defined in the tangent left-gauge as

$$ \delta\langle V_{b}\rangle=\tr(M_{b}W+M_{b}^{\dagger}W^{\dagger})\,, $$

which can be shown to take the form

$$ M_{b}=\int dx\,\left(-r_{bJ,bJ}l^{\dagger}_{bJ,bJ}R^{\dagger}+r_{bJ,bJ}R^{\dagger}l^{\dagger}_{bJ,bJ}+bJ(x)r_{bJ,bJ}l^{\dagger}_{bJ,bJ}\right)\,. $$

Similar expressions can be derived for $\langle\mathcal{O}_{n}\rangle$ and $\langle\mathcal{H}_{\text{free}}\rangle$ . To determine the direction of steepest descent one needs to define a metric on the tangent vectors. There are two natural options: the standard Euclidean metric $\tr(W^{\dagger}W)$ and the Hilbert space metric (3.11). In left-gauge ( $l=\mathds{1}$ ), these metrics give rise to the following steepest descent directions

$$ \displaystyle\text{Euclidean metric:} \displaystyle W \displaystyle=-M_{b}^{\dagger}\,, \displaystyle\text{Hilbert space metric:} \displaystyle W \displaystyle=-M_{b}^{\dagger}r^{-1}\,. $$

The numerical minimization is performed using the limited-memory Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (LBFGS) algorithm, as implemented in OptimKit.jl, loosely following the implementation in [43]. In particular, we use the standard Euclidean metric for LBFGS and implement the non-trivial Hilbert space metric (C.4) as a preconditioner for the descent step. The matrix inversion $r^{-1}$ in the preconditioner can be ill-conditioned and is therefore regularized as $(r^{2}+\epsilon^{2})^{-1/2}$ , with the regulator $\epsilon$ proportional to the norm of the gradient. Furthermore, following [43], we prepare the initial state by running LBFGS for $\sim 50-100$ iterations without the preconditioner.

Once the vacuum RCMPS is determined, we solve for the low-lying eigenvalues of the effective Hamiltonian (3.21). To compute the soliton spectrum, we need to determine two RCMPSs representing the two degenerate vacua between which the soliton interpolates. From a given vacuum, we can determine the other degenerate vacuum by explicitly acting with the spontaneously broken symmetry operators on the RCMPS ansatz (see Appendix D for details). This procedure also fixes the momentum ambiguity described below (3.65), because the left and right vacua are related, and therefore cannot be rephased independently. After the two degenerate vacua have been found, the soliton masses are again extracted by diagonalizing the effective Hamiltonian.

## Appendix D Symmetries and RCMPSs

In this appendix, we will derive the action of symmetry transformations on the RCMPS ansatz relevant for the sine-Gordon and $\phi^{4}$ theories.

### D.1 $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ reflection symmetry

In both sine-Gordon and $\phi^{4}$ theories, $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ reflection is implemented by a unitary operator $U$ that acts on the operators $\phi,\pi$ as

$$ U^{\dagger}\phi(x)U=-\phi(x)\,,\qquad U^{\dagger}\pi(x)U=-\pi(x)\,. $$

The definition (2.7) implies that $U^{\dagger}a^{\dagger}(x)U=-a^{\dagger}(x)$ , and so the action of $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ reflection on an RCMPS is

$$ \displaystyle U|Q,R\rangle \displaystyle=v_{L}^{\dagger}U\mathcal{P}\exp\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,Q\otimes\mathds{1}+R\otimes a^{\dagger}(x)\right]U^{\dagger}v_{R}U|0\rangle=|Q,-R\rangle\,, $$

where we used that the Fock vacuum is invariant under $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ reflection $U|0\rangle=|0\rangle$ . It is easily seen that the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ reflection transformation

$$ (Q,R)\mapsto(Q,-R) $$

preserves the left-gauge condition (2.26). Consequently, one does not have to regauge the RCMPS after applying (D.3).

### D.2 Shift symmetry

The sine-Gordon theory (4.1) is also invariant under discrete shifts of $\phi$ . The shift transformations by some amount $\alpha$ act as

$$ U^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\phi(x)U_{\alpha}=\phi(x)+\alpha\,,\qquad U^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\pi(x)U_{\alpha}=\pi(x)\,, $$

and it is explicitly realized by

$$ U_{\alpha}\equiv e^{-i\alpha\int dy\,\pi(y)}=e^{\Delta\int dy\,(a^{\dagger}(y)-a(y))}\,, $$

where we defined $\Delta\equiv\alpha{\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{2}}}$ and in the second equality used (2.5) and (2.7). To compute $U_{\alpha}|Q,R\rangle$ , we need the action of $U_{\alpha}$ on $a^{\dagger}(x)$ and $|0\rangle$ . For the Fock vacuum, we use (D.5) and split the exponent using the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula

$$ U_{\alpha}|0\rangle=e^{-\int dx\frac{\Delta^{2}}{2}}e^{\Delta\int dx\,a^{\dagger}(x)}|0\rangle\,. $$

For the operator $a^{\dagger}(x)$ , we have the commutation relation $[\int dy\,(a^{\dagger}(y)-a(y)),a^{\dagger}(x)]=-1$ which implies that

$$ U^{\dagger}_{\alpha}a^{\dagger}(x)U_{\alpha}=a^{\dagger}(x)+\Delta\,, $$

Putting together (D.6) and (D.7), we deduce the action of the shift operator on the RCMPS ansatz

$$ \displaystyle U_{\alpha}|Q,R\rangle=|Q-\Delta R-\frac{\Delta^{2}}{2}\mathds{1},R+\Delta\mathds{1}\rangle\,. $$

This transformation of $(Q,R)$ also preserves the left-gauge condition (2.26).

## Appendix E Effective quantum mechanics

In this appendix, we give further details on the matching of the amplitude (4.11) and the effective non-relativistic Hamiltonian by considering $2\rightarrow 2$ scattering of the elementary excitation.

The scattering amplitude corresponding to the tree-level diagrams (4.11) computed using the Feynman rules derived from (4.6) is

$$ i\mathcal{M}_{\text{tree}}=-24ig-72ig\widetilde{m}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{s-\widetilde{m}^{2}}+\frac{1}{t-\widetilde{m}^{2}}+\frac{1}{u-\widetilde{m}^{2}}\right)\,, $$

where $s,t,u$ are the Mandelstam variables. We will consider the scattering in the center-of-momentum frame, with incoming spatial momentum $p$ and outgoing spatial momentum $q$ , with $p=\pm q$ . The Mandelstam variables are

$$ s=4(\tilde{m}^{2}+p^{2})\,,\qquad t=-2(p^{2}-pq)\,,\qquad u=-2(p^{2}+pq)\,. $$

Expanding the amplitude for small momenta, we find the result (4.11) quoted in the main text:

$$ i\mathcal{M}_{\text{tree}}=96ig+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{p^{2}}{\widetilde{m}^{2}}\right)\,. $$

We want to relate this amplitude to the amplitude computed in an effective quantum mechanics problem that governs the relative motion of the particles in the center-of-momentum frame. In particular, we want to match a Hamiltonian of the form

$$ H_{\text{NR}}=\frac{p^{2}}{\widetilde{m}}+V(x)\,, $$

where $\widetilde{m}/2$ is the reduced mass, and $V(x)$ is the two-particle interaction potential, which we need to determine. To deduce $V(x)$ , we start from the relation between the S-matrix and the invariant amplitude [44]

$$ \langle q_{1},q_{2}|S-\mathds{1}|p_{1},p_{2}\rangle_{\text{QFT}}=(2\pi)^{2}\delta(\omega_{q_{1}}+\omega_{q_{2}}-\omega_{p_{1}}-\omega_{p_{2}})\,\delta(q_{1}+q_{2}-p_{1}-p_{2})\,i\mathcal{M}\,, $$

with the relativistic normalization

$$ \langle q_{1},q_{2}|p_{1},p_{2}\rangle_{\text{QFT}}=(2\omega_{p_{1}})(2\omega_{p_{2}})(2\pi)^{2}\left[\delta(q_{1}-p_{1})\delta(q_{2}-p_{2})+\delta(q_{1}-p_{2})\delta(q_{2}-p_{1})\right]\,. $$

Here, the two sets of delta functions are due to Bose symmetry. In the center-of-momentum frame, $p_{1}=-p_{2}=p$ and $q_{1}=-q_{2}=q$ , so (E.5) becomes

$$ \langle q,-q|S-\mathds{1}|p,-p\rangle_{\text{QFT}}=(2\pi)^{2}\delta(0)\,\delta(2\omega_{q}-2\omega_{p})\,i\mathcal{M}\,. $$

We compare the tree-level approximation of (E.7) with the lowest-order (Born approximation) S-matrix element of the effective quantum mechanics, obtained from the Lippmann-Schwinger equation [45],

$$ \langle q,-q|S-\mathds{1}|p,-p\rangle_{\text{NR}}=-i(2\pi)^{2}\delta(0)\,\delta(E_{q}-E_{p})\left(\langle q|V|p\rangle+\langle q|V|-p\rangle\right), $$

where $E_{p}=p^{2}/\widetilde{m}$ is the non-relativistic energy from (E.4), and the second term is the exchange contribution arising from the Bose-symmetric normalization

$$ \langle q_{1},q_{2}|p_{1},p_{2}\rangle_{\text{NR}}=(2\pi)^{2}\left[\delta(q_{1}-p_{1})\delta(q_{2}-p_{2})+\delta(q_{1}-p_{2})\delta(q_{2}-p_{1})\right]. $$

The matching condition is therefore

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\langle q,-q|S-\mathds{1}|p,-p\rangle_{\text{QFT}}}{4\omega_{p}^{2}} \displaystyle=(2\pi)^{2}\delta(0)\,\delta(2\omega_{q}-2\omega_{p})\,\frac{i\mathcal{M}_{\text{tree}}}{4\omega_{p}^{2}} \displaystyle\overset{!}{=}-i(2\pi)^{2}\delta(0)\,\delta(E_{q}-E_{p})\left(\langle q|V|p\rangle+\langle q|V|-p\rangle\right). $$

For $p,q\ll\widetilde{m}$ , we have $\omega_{p}\approx\widetilde{m}$ and $2\omega_{q}-2\omega_{p}\approx E_{q}-E_{p}$ , and the delta functions cancel. With $\mathcal{M}_{\text{tree}}=96g$ as in (E.3), this gives

$$ \langle q|V|p\rangle+\langle q|V|-p\rangle=-\frac{24g}{\widetilde{m}^{2}}\,,\qquad V(x)=-\frac{12g}{\widetilde{m}^{2}}\,\delta(x)\,. $$

For $g>0$ , the potential is attractive and has a single bound state with energy $-\frac{36g^{2}}{\widetilde{m}^{3}}$ . Moreover, its wavefunction is symmetric, as required by Bose symmetry.
